I welcome the opportunity provided by this examination of the estimates of the Department of Public Works to comment briefly on housing, and in particular on the statement made by the minister Monday morning in respect to changes in the

Supply-Public Works maximum income level regulations and respecting merchant builders' loans.
I suggest that this statement by the government was long overdue and is a recognition, finally, after many months of stalling, of the mess in which this government has placed the residential construction industry, the people engaged in it, and the thousands of people throughout Canada who still require better housing.
In this respect I should like to quote briefly from an article in the Calgary Herald of July 6 which quotes Mr. John Smith, executive vice-president of National House Builders' Association, as saying in Alberta:
In so far as getting houses built, the federal government policy of confining National Housing Act direct loans to individual owner-applicants has been a "resounding fizzle".
Later he said:
Assuming that the government wants to avoid a housing shortage, with the rise in prices this would mean, revision of its restrictive policy is needed.
Now to return to the statement of the minister which, although carefully worded, admits the dilemma in which this government finds itself after three years of unplanned activity in housing. When the economy began to sag in the fall of 1957 this government pumped money into housing at unprecedented levels. That had the result of artificially overexpanding the house building industry and building in 1958 many of the houses required in 1959. The use of housing to prime the economic pump, while having the effect of building a great many houses, was not a normal development.
The results are evident in certain areas even today. Many areas were vastly overbuilt, and many other areas throughout the country received little or no benefit. It is these areas that did not share in this housing boom that were the first to suffer when the government realized the mess it had got itself into. Hon. members on all sides are very much aware of this situation.
The regulations imposed this year were deliberately restrictive and have had a paralyzing effect on house building in many areas. With the imposition of these restrictive regulations by the government, the areas that need housing cannot produce the normal demand while certain other areas that were overbuilt in 1958 still have many unsold homes.
There are many reasons for this unhappy state of affairs, most of which are the responsibility of this government. Prior to 1957 it was the policy of the then federal government to assume the role, in the main, of residual lender. It is interesting to note that in 1956, a year of real expansion and economic boom, Canadians were able to build

135,700 homes through normal demand. However, late in 1957, when the economy began to slip, this government used housing in an effort to bolster the economy, and no one will argue seriously against their action at that time.
The extent to which such actions should be employed is of course debatable. The results of these past few years clearly indicate the degree of control that can be exercised over housing and the economy by a federal government. When it appears that total activity might lag, house building can be stimulated; when it appears that total activity in the economy might strain our total resources, steps can be taken to curtail house building. As I said just a moment ago, the extent to which this stimulation or curtailment might be applied is, of course, debatable.
The power of the federal government to control the rate of house building is made possible largely through its control over the National Housing Act mortgage market, which controls the supply of mortgage funds by making the National Housing Act rates attractive or unattractive to private lenders, by varying the volume of its own lendings. Changes in interest rates affect the public demand for N.H.A. loans.
Naturally there are many other factors, but it is not my intention to go into too much detail at this time in the general field of housing, as we have discussed the subject rather thoroughly on other occasions during this session. I intend to content myself today with pointing out again, as I have on several occasions during this session, the failure of the government in this important field of activity.
The minister's statement on Monday can be considered little more than an admission of the failure of the government's announced 1960 housing program. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that when we discussed housing legislation back in February and March the government stated that its minimum objective was 125,000 housing starts in 1960. At the same time it announced, while asking parliament for $500 million, that only $175 million would be used in 1960. As we pointed out at that time, this was a 50 per cent reduction as compared with the amount advanced in 1959.
This was a ridiculously restrictive attitude taken by the government at a time when all other lending for house construction was being curtailed for various reasons. The banks were knocked out of lending for house construction by government action, and the approved lenders could place their money elsewhere at more attractive rates as a result of the tight money situation created earlier

by this same government. Surely this year was the time when government lending for house building should have been advanced to a degree that would cushion the hardships created by the curtailment of lending, for the reasons I have outlined above, by the normal suppliers of mortgage funds.
You will also remember, sir, that this government were not satisfied merely to slash in half the amount that would be advanced through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at this time of curtailment, but they went further in their ridiculously restrictive measures. By putting on a ceiling of $5,000, plus minor adjustments depending on the number of children in a family, the government further restricted their lending. At the time it was introduced some of us on this side expressed the view that it was a mistake. My own view was that this was a gimmick dreamed up by the government for public consumption, to create an impression that something was being done for the so-called little man while in effect nothing was being done. With a ceiling of $5,000 and the minimum wage requirement throughout the country near this figure, they left a very narrow area of wage earners who could even qualify. When one considers this wage ceiling restriction and the minimum salary requirement, plus the substantial down payment required, it is little wonder that this deliberately restrictive housing program of the government in 1960 failed throughout.
This recent announcement by the government recognizes this failure which has resulted from this government's misjudgment and failure to correctly analyse developments over the past several months. I realize the government hoped that construction outside the housing field would take up the slack resulting from the government's deliberate reduction of house construction. It has become increasingly apparent with each passing month that the government's hopes in this regard were not to be realized. Each month produced a new set of figures, in fact set new records of reduction in house building. This has not only resulted in the loss of construction but has had the effect of contributing substantially to a greater number of failures among construction companies in the first quarter of this year than in any similar previous period.
It is a matter of record that in no one field is there more unemployment than among residential construction workers. Therefore it is little wonder that the government are attempting now, at this late date, to make
79951-0-415i
Supply-Public Works up for their failure in handling the construction program for 1960. This cautious statement by the government makes reference to the dilemma in which the government finds itself at this time. The statement indicates that they do not wish to produce more housing to be added to the present stock of unsold dwellings, yet they recognize that to restrict house building is in effect to restrict employment opportunities. Therefore, after months of stalling, after months of drifting, the government have faced up to their 1960 failure and are now prepared to make an upward revision in the income limitations on applicants, and to release a few more million dollars. By their action they hope to beef up their 1960 program.
It is difficult at this time to tell what effect this change will have in respect of additional starts in 1960, and I know that the minister with all his experts was not prepared to make a forecast in this connection. However the fact that the merchant builders' aspect does not come into effect until September 1, and will be cancelled at the end of November, would seem to indicate that the government is still hedging, still trying to cut down on the amount of funds to be advanced through direct lending. The statement also indicates that after November 30, only home owner applications will be received, on terms and conditions to be announced at that time.
It is difficult to assess the real significance behind this proposed piecemeal action. The terms and conditions referred to in the statement, that are to be made known in November, may well reflect the government's thinking and timing in respect of the next election. However, of two things we can be sure; the government's recognition of the failure of its present policy and also that the government recognizes the levelling off that is taking place in our economy.
As has been clearly shown in recent years, the volume of house building responds quickly to changes in the quantity, availability and terms of N.H.A. mortgage money. The house building industry is a major employer of labour and for the most part uses materials produced in our own country. There are also such things as appliances and home furnishings required, each adding to employment generally. The cutting back on house building in times of prosperity releases considerable manpower and materials for other sectors of the economy. The stimulating of house building in a recession has the reverse effect; at least this is the theory.
The evils or difficulties lie in a policy of attempting to produce total stability by artificially and deliberately creating instability in house building. These violent fluctuations, this

Supply-Public Works turning on and off of the tap of mortgage funds, are very costly. The availability of mortgage money in a state of feast or famine has created a great degree of instability in the house building industry.
During these past few months we have experienced one of these famine periods in respect of the availability of mortgage money, created in no small degree by government policy and government action. During the past several months the approved lenders under N.H.A. have found investment in other fields much more attractive. In the first six months of 1960 the approved lenders made 7,364 loans as compared with 19,730 loans in the first quarter of 1959. This represents a decrease of 62.7 per cent. Since the N.H.A. rate was raised last fall to 6| per cent the chartered banks have been understandably reluctant to make loans at 6 per cent, which is their limit under the Bank Act. As a result only 41 loans were made by the chartered banks in the first six months of this year, as compared with 11,302 in the first six months of 1959.
As I said, it was during this period of restriction of the normal sources of mortgage lending that the government should have been prepared to take up at least a portion of the slack. Instead they sat there, trying to deny the failure of their policy, shirking their responsibility and endeavouring by insinuation to shift to others the blame and responsibility that were theirs.
I would like to refer to one shining example of this attempt to shift responsibility. Hon. members will recall a statement made by the hon. member for Carleton to the effect that the Canadian lending institutions had abdicated their social responsibilities. This quotable mouthful, delivered at a party meeting, I suggest was a carefully thought out scheme to shift the blame from the government to the lending institutions. This statement made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance could not avoid being associated with government thinking in that important department of government. Yet, under questioning in the house, the minister assumed his usual role and would not agree or disagree with the statement by his parliamentary secretary.
These tactics by a frustrated government trying to get out from under their responsibilities did not fool many people. I suggest if there was any abdication of responsibility it is this government which has abdicated. I suggest that by their inaction and their decision to restrict house building in 1960 they have kept Canadian labour unemployed in an attempt to save funds in sufficient volume for a special boost to the economy whenever they decide it may be necessary.
There is much I could say on the government's handling of housing. That they have

used housing there can be no denying. The minister's statement on Monday admitted this meddling, when he said, "The present direct lending policy was restricted for fiscal reasons". Earlier in the session the minister admitted in the house, and I quote his words, that the government had "ruined the mortgage market".
Now, at the pinnacle of their failure, they come forward with an announcement they hope will get them off the hook. We see evidence of it already. The Minister of Labour has already used in the house the statement of the Minister of Public Works as the government's answer to fuller employment.
Part of the answer.

The Minister of Public Works has been on television already announcing to his captive audience this sedative being offered the public in the hope that they will forget the painful sobering up period after the two-year housing binge engaged in by the government. However, no juggling of figures can absolve the government from the responsibility for causing unnecessary hardships in the house building industry and among our unemployed citizens this year. The figures each month for the first half of the year have reflected the failure of the government's 1960 housing program.
It might be of interest to put on the record some of these figures. I should like to quote from "Canadian Housing Statistics", a monthly publication of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It is interesting to note that in the first line of their brief comment they say that housing starts turned upward in June. Housing starts were not up in June; in fact they are down 23 per cent, to 8,706 from 11,319 last year. They are up only in the sense that they are not down as sharply as they were in May.
I should like to refer to the key figures very briefly on the year to date. As of June 30 this year starts were down 34.7 per cent. All N.H.A. loans throughout Canada were down 62.2 per cent. Approved lenders' loans were down 62.7 per cent. In that field chartered bank loans were down 99.6 per cent and corporation loans were down 61.3 per cent.
The instability caused by this failure can only mean increased costs for new housing and in turn higher prices for those purchasing older homes. Surely, with costs at an all-time high, the government should not be engaged in policies that are adding to these costs. Surely this was one period, when other lenders were restricting their activities, for the government to come forward if the public

requiring housing were to be given any consideration. However, fiscal considerations, as confirmed by the minister's statement, were the prime consideration of the government as it drifts toward its fourth straight deficit.
During a period of approximately two years the government has been up to its ears in housing, supplying hundreds of millions of dollars which artificially stimulated the industry. I believe they have recognized the folly of their ways and are anxious to resume the role of residual lenders. If this is the case, their withdrawal should have been more orderly and more gradual to avoid unnecessary instability in the house building industry.
I have other matters I wish to discuss with respect to the department's estimates, but I propose to do so on the specific items.

Mr. Chairman, the minister
seems to be coming in for a lot of criticism. Personally I should like to thank him for what he has done in my constituency and a great many others throughout the country. First of all, one little point that I think bears mentioning has to do with the attitude of the minister and his predecessor toward the safety of tourists on the waters in the Okanagan valley and on other lakes. The lakes there are extremely turbulent, and a series of breakwaters have been built for various communities. Penticton and Kelowna have had extensions, and Summerland and Peachland have had new breakwaters. In fact Summerland has had an extension to its new one already. These works, along with various public buildings now in the course of construction and proposed for the future, have done a lot to relieve unemployment and a great deal for the valley and the safety of tourists on the waters of the lakes.
I listened to the last speaker, the hon. member for Nipissing, and I was a little astounded. He is a man who is very interested in house building, C.M.H.C. loans and so on. It seems to me that a great many people in the Liberal party take a lot of pleasure in slamming the present government for its housing policy. I do not want to go into statistics, except to state that the total amount made available for housing now has reached $1,500 million, and to point out that at June, 1957 the total available was $150 million of which only approximately $100 million had been used. That is a great difference. In 1957, at a time when it was greatly required, housing had come to a virtual standstill. I know that in my own constituency of Okanagan Boundary builders wanted money for housing and could not get it. I would remind hon. members again that of the $150 million which had been set aside, only $100 million had been used.
Supply-Public Works Today over $1 billion has been made available under C.M.H.C. and there is an additional $500 million available if and when the need becomes apparent.
For these reasons I feel that the Minister of Public Works did a good deed for Canada in his original announcement, and also in his recent announcement increasing the amount of loans. This will do a great deal not only for housing in Canada and for the people of Canada but also for those in the trades connected with building who are unemployed.

Mr. Chairman, since we are discussing and approving the estimates of the Minister of Public Works, I should like to bring to his attention some of the problems in my area and also make some remarks about the policy of his department and the government pertaining to the housing situation in Canada.
In contrast to some speakers who have waited until the end of their speeches to offer congratulations to the minister and the officers of his department, possibly I may assist him to have a moment of respite before I discuss the matters I have in mind by saying that I am pleased to extend my thanks to him for the many services he has had occasion to render to me on behalf of the citizens of Nickel Belt when I have had occasion to correspond with him. This also applies to his departmental officials with whom I have had contact concerning these same problems.
I do not wish to indicate by these words that Nickel Belt has received all that it requires. Nor by referring to certain works which were undertaken and which have been finished since the estimates of the minister were last before the house do I wish to indicate that Nickel Belt is necessarily the pet of the minister. I am pleased to state to him that the citizens of my constituency have had occasion to rejoice because of some of the works which were requested and which have been completed. For instance, there is the dock at Eighteen Mile island on the French river. Undoubtedly members of the house will recognize that northern Ontario is definitely one place in the province where expansion of the tourist trade is required and can be accomplished, and it is by means of these facilities that this can be done.
Recently I had occasion to visit the site at Eighteen Mile island, and the dock is definitely a proper one although it suffered certain damage during the course of last winter. I am sure that by now that damage has been repaired. It is true also that the citizens are enjoying the facilities which have been constructed in Boland's bay in lake

Supply-Public Works Wanapitei, where extensive repairs had to be undertaken. I trust the minister will also indicate to the committee whether the work has been completed by his department at Gogama.

Gogama; there is correspondence between me and the minister on that. I have not had time to visit the location this year to see whether the work has been completed.
There is one more specific problem with which I should like to deal at this time. I refer to the problem facing the citizens of Foleyet in my riding. Reference has been made in this house to the flood which unfortunately occurred there last May. Many questions were asked, and I have had occasion to try to obtain information from the minister concerning responsibility for the dam which broke and caused the drastic flood. This was not the ordinary type of mishap or the ordinary type of flood which might be occasioned by too much rainfall. The citizens of Foleyet have given me certain details concerning the events at the time the dam broke at Ivanhoe lake.
I had occasion to receive information from the minister concerning the part of the federal government played in the construction of this dam. If I may refer the minister to Hansard for June 29 last, page 5528, he will note that his answer indicated that the federal government, under the Bennett regime in 1931, undertook to pay one third of the cost of constructing the dam.
If one visits the flood area some people will tell you that the homes and furnishings lost were not of the expensive type. However, many of these people in Foleyet are elderly people and the homes and goods which they lost possibly represented their life savings, so the loss sustained was quite drastic. I can tell the minister that the result of the flood in some areas in Foleyet has been to practically bring about a new river bed. I know that where one home existed which I would value at between $6,000 and $7,000, there now exists a river possibly 15 feet or 20 feet deep. Through field glasses I could see the house which used to be there, about one mile away in a swamp. Undoubtedly many persons lost their homes, their furniture and even the ground upon which they built their homesteads.
It was stated by the Prime Minister, and possibly the Minister of Public Works, on one occasion that if the provincial government requested some assistance in providing relief for the area the federal government would 

give consideration to such a request. I suggest that since the dam which broke and caused the flood was constructed partly with federal assistance, then the federal government has some responsibility in the matter. I would think the federal government would be on at least the same footing as certain charitable institutions which were giving help to the town. I have tried to obtain some information from the provincial minister of lands and forests who undoubtedly, if the newspaper reports are correct, was the person in charge of estimating the damages and finding ways and means of assisting the area, but I have received no reply from the provincial minister.
I have quite an extensive file in connection with this matter. Many of the citizens have written to me indicating the position in which they find themselves. They indicate to me that within a few hours of this occurrence there was water in many homes up to the ceilings. So far as I have been able to ascertain, the provincial authorities have requested the citizens to see their priests and ministers in order to obtain charity through the organization of bingos and raffles. This situation is a bad one; it is a bad one for these citizens. Long before now this government should have been in communication with the provincial authorities so that at least this government could be considered as being on the same footing as those organizations putting on the raffles and bingos to help these citizens.
I say that a degree of responsibility falls upon the federal government as the result of participation in the construction of the dam, so the minister should bring about the required investigation, along with the department of lands and forests of the province of Ontario, to make sure assistance is rendered these people in a manner which they can understand. Some of the letters I have received from these citizens indicate that they are at a loss to know how to organize themselves in order to ascertain who is responsible for the damages they have sustained. There should be some investigation to ascertain responsibility, and the citizens should be properly informed.
There is another problem, Mr. Chairman, to which I should like to refer, and that is the French river flood which was discussed in this house some months ago. This flood is connected with the dam which was built at the mouth of the French river where it enters lake Nipissing. The dam, of course, creates certain probleins during the time when the excess water from lake Nipissing is draining through the river in the early spring. The problem arises partly because

the river has not been dredged or some other precuation taken to allow for this excess water.
I realize that this is a major project. I realize that studies have to be made. However, we are told that the government is presently considering the feasibility of having the waters from James bay taken through certain channels on down the French river into Georgian bay and the great lakes. It seems to me that it would be proper for the minister, in connection with the investigations which are being made, to ascertain what can be done in the lower sections of the French river so that the water could readily flow into the great lakes without occasioning damage or problems for the operators in these areas. While we have heard of the Kearns report which is at present before the government, necessarily part of it should pertain to the French river in my area which undoubtedly will be part of the entire scheme and where major improvements should be made.
A further problem-and I am sure the minister will see that possibly an investigation is made on the same and remedies brought about to solve it-is the matter of the trans-Canada highway which runs south from Sudbury. There is a stretch from Sudbury to Burwash which has developed a condition which is known as a soupy surface and where many accidents have occurred which were rather difficult to explain except for the condition of the highway on rainy days. I am sure that if the government was prepared to pay over 50 per cent of the cost of that highway it is also entitled to ascertain that it is being properly constructed. If an improvement is to be brought about, I hope it will make the proper arrangements with the province to make the trans-Canada highway, in which it plays a part, proper and safe for the citizens using the same.
As I indicated earlier, it is my intention to discuss with the minister and the committee at this time certain aspects of the policy of this government concerning Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the lending through that agency to the Canadian public for the purpose of promoting house building in Canada. I realize that there is possibly not a more important problem for the average citizen than that of the possibility of obtaining a home for himself. Housing should be considered-and I trust the minister will still consider it-in Canada as one of the major projects. I hope the minister will make greater efforts and better efforts to emulate the previous government which did so much for housing in Canada.
Housing in itself is most important. Citizens really feel that they achieve something when
Supply-Public Works they obtain a home for themselves and their families. But over and above that consideration there is the problem of unemployment which housing in a great respect can solve.
I have stated previously in this chamber, and I state it again, that in my area unemployment was to a great degree over the last 12 months due to the lack of housing projects being undertaken in that area.
If I may, I should like to refer the minister to the table which we received yesterday on unemployment. He will note that unemployment is still 20 per cent higher in June, 1960 than it was in June, 1959 and unemployment was grave at that time. If the minister refers to table 2 of the dominion bureau of statistics figures which we received yesterday afternoon, he will find that statement to be absolutely true. I must state that my area, namely the area of Sudbury and Nickel Belt, is a classic example of the grave increase in the unemployment in 1960 over 1959. In our area we have a 20 per cent increase in the unemployment figures at the unemployment office in Sudbury which covers my area. For that reason I have stated also that the major cause of this situation was a lack of construction promotion in my area as well as in other areas of Canada.
For these reasons, namely the solution of unemployment and the need of the Canadian people, I think it is true to say that this government has failed gravely in this respect in properly promoting the construction of residential buildings in Canada. I believe there is no worse black mark against the minister than the policy which he initiated concerning housing in Canada a very few months ago. We all recall-and it is no secret to this committee-how the Liberal opposition fought a few months ago when the new regulations were indicated to the house by the Minister of Public Works. I think it was a fallacy for him yesterday, in presenting the new regulations, to state simply that from month to month conditions vary in Canada. When he made the statement as to releasing more moneys and making more applicants free to apply for loans from C.M.H.C., I think it was a definite admission of the failure of the policies he initiated in this chamber a short time ago.
At that time the Liberal party opposition made it clear that they felt that the regulations initiated at that time by the Minister of Public Works would not do. I am sure the minister has received, as well as have I, reproaches from the citizens of my area and other areas in the country. I think that when he said that conditions have changed from June, this is just an alibi for an explanation which he should give the house in stating that the policies initiated a short time ago

Supply-Public Works would not suffice for the needs of our country. I think he finds himself today possibly in the same position as that of a shoemaker making great efforts to try to build a lady's shoe which would be larger on the inside than on the outside. Although he tries to pretend that the policies of this government were sufficient, it is obvious to us that in no way were they such. I say that the date to which he now has opened the new regulations, namely September 1, is too late and there are many reasons for that.
I had occasion to criticize the regulations initiated by the Minister of Public Works some time ago as affecting more drastically than others the area which I represent. That was true on account of the ceiling he had placed on the income of those who could apply for loans. I say that the new regulation which is set out by him in his statement made to the house yesterday indicates that certain areas such as northern Ontario will be drastically affected. Now we are wanting to make home construction or residential construction a wintertime affair. I agree that in many types of work, winter works projects may be of some value. But to say that an ordinary man's home, the cost of which may vary from $8,000 to $14,000, is a project which you can put through in the wintertime without any loss to the home owner or without any extra cost to the home owner is, in my opinion, to make a faulty statement. A house costing $8,000 or $14,000 is not in the domain of a building costing $1 million which definitely may be built in a year and a half and therefore is proper to have the work done in two winters and one summer. But a house for an ordinary man is not in the same category. In northern Ontario it is definite that you will add extremely to the cost of a house if you undertake the building of it during the winter.
Furthermore, if I understand the regulation put out by the minister yesterday, it states that a man must be an actual buyer. A man who knows the design of the house and wants that house before it is started, that person, for the purpose of speculation, will not be able to operate. This regulation therefore makes it definite that the man who wants a home built will be a man who will be living in it. If it is built during the wintertime in northern Ontario there is no doubt you will have to heat the house. In order to heat a house which is new, where the windows are not necessarily all installed and where possibly you have something else in the windows outside of the glass that should go in them, if you heat the house it will cost you in the neighbourhood of $40 or $50 a month.

For a house under construction in northern Ontario this will necessarily add $100 to the cost and that is not the only cost which must be added to the cost of the house which is built in the wintertime. There are other factors to be considered as well. For instance, there is the matter of bringing in sewers to the house in the wintertime. That is something that adds to the cost.
I think it is very wrong that the minister should have hesitated in accepting the Liberal policy explained some two or three months ago, and hardships will result due to the reluctance on the part of the minister to accept the advice of the Liberal opposition.
Furthermore, very few people decide to obtain a new home in September or October. That major decision is usually made during the summer months when the children are out of school. People readily admit they prefer to construct a new home in the springtime, in May or June, rather than in September or October. I do not say there are no exceptions but it is reasonable to assume the majority of the citizens who are thinking of a new home will make the move when the children leave school and before another term is started. I think this is another problem on the shoulders of the Minister of Public Works.
The citizens in my riding are happy that at long last the minister and this government has seen fit to enlarge the scope of the building industry in Canada, and especially in my area. However, I must state that the people in my area realize the harm this government has done to the home building industry by its conduct during the last few months. I am happy to speak after the hon. member for Nipissing who made such a clear expose of the present situation in northern Ontario and Canada with regard to housing. He also underlined the full responsibility of this government and its policies with regard to the very bad statistics which have resulted in drops of 64 per cent, 34 per cent and 32 per cent.
I may say in closing that there is no comparison between the housing situation in Canada in 1960 and any other period during the last Liberal administration.
Oh, oh.

There cannot be. The unemployment in my area is due in very great part to the situation with regard to the construction of homes and the building industry itself. Plumbers are unemployed and the carpenters are unemployed. Fortunately we have good mining in northern Ontario and the mines are operating at the present time. But I have to come before this committee to state that unemployment has increased 20 per cent, and

I must find the reason for that. The people of my area are finding the reason and the reason lies with the policies of the government, a government which said no one would suffer. What the government has done to housing can be seen by anyone on the sidewalks as they go through my riding, and unemployment is found especially in the home building industry.
For these reasons I say that the problem is grave. If it is any comfort to the minister we are happy that he takes some glory for the present regulation. I cannot stress the fact any further that a short time ago the Liberal opposition pressed for this. If it satisfies the minister to say he did this on his own, although he has had days and days of criticism, then let him take the glory, and if construction does continue in the way we would like to see it continue it will be of some assistance. I am sure that if prosperity is brought back the unemployment situation will be remedied to a great extent, and we will definitely be happy in Nickel Belt.

On behalf of the people in my constituency, especially the Kitchener chamber of commerce, the public utilities commission, the mayor and the city council, I should like to express our thanks to the minister, his deputy and the department for the wonderful co-operation we have received in recent negotiations concerning the site for a new post office.
I could add much more to my remarks but I do not want to delay the estimates. I merely say again to the minister, his deputy and the department-thanks a million.

Mr. Chairman, there are two general subjects I should like to bring to the attention of the minister in the consideration of his estimates. The first has to do with a question I asked in the opening days of the session but because of the regulation of questions on orders of the day and other considerations I was unable to obtain an answer which I considered to be adequate.
The minister will recall that on January 19, 1960, as reported on page 82 of Hansard, after having considerable difficulty in putting my question across I did ask the minister this question:
Is It still the intention of the Minister of Public Works to permit members of the Conservative party to have the privilege of announcing public works projects in their ridings, when this privilege is denied to members of the Liberal or C.C.F. parties?
The Minister of Public Works answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for his congratulations, and to say that it is most difficult to give a definite answer to a hypothetical question.
79951-0-416
Supply-Public Works
I did not agree with the minister at the time nor do I now that my question was in any way hypothetical. As a matter of fact one of the reasons I brought the question up in the first place was because of the statement reported to have been made by the minister to the effect that the subject matter of my question had been stated by him. Indeed the newspapers at that time carried articles on his statement.
As a matter of fact in the Ottawa Citizen of September 24, 1959 there is an article entitled "Tory MPs to share in glory", and it goes on:
Conservative MPs are going to get a share of the glory attached to the granting of federal works contracts in their constituencies.
The new public works minister David Walker has come up with a system of coupling his own name with that of the MP concerned in information released on contracts.
The announcements now read that "John Doe, MP, announces on behalf of public works minister Walker, etc., etc."
I do not have to interject here, I am sure, that the "John Doe, MP" is of necessity a Conservative member.
The article goes on to say:
While no one in the department has said so, it can be assumed that where a contract is let in a constituency represented by a Liberal or C.C.F. member, the publicity release will carry Mr. Walker's name only.
I do not think my question was hypothetical at the time I asked it. As a matter of fact, ever since the minister has been in office it seems to me that is the policy he has carried out. It is a policy which, to use the most euphemistic term, can only be qualified as extreme political partisanship. I, in my riding, together, I am sure, with other members of the Liberal party have not been made aware of any of the projects which have been contemplated by the Department of Public Works, nor have I been kept informed, as I should have been, about the works which have been completed. Moreover I strongly suspect that although the privilege of announcing public works in their ridings has been refused some hon. members who have been elected to this house, defeated Conservative candidates have been given that privilege. It seems to me that the government is forgetting that all members of this house have been duly elected by their constituents and that they have not only the responsibility but the right to know what is going on in their ridings. I do not know of any legal or constitutional justification-indeed, I do not know of any justification- for a defeated candidate being given privileges denied to elected members of the Liberal and C.C.F. party.
I wonder whether the minister thinks that this policy which apparently he is following

Supply-Public Works adds anything to the dignity or to the objectivity of parliament? It creates two classes of members of parliament, one a privileged class and one an under-privileged class. I believe it is a most unfair and most undemocratic procedure. It is contrary to the speeches which have been made so many times in this house by members and supporters of the government about their concern for the rights and dignity of hon. members, and I hope that if the government and the minister intend to continue the policy which has been followed up until now they will at least spare us any further sanctimonious if not hypocritical speeches about the dignity and rights of members of parliament.
The second subject to which I should like to refer briefly is one in which I am very interested as, I am sure, are other members in the house and many citizens of this country as well as of the United States. It has to do with the Richelieu waterway. The other day the minister said a review of this project was being made. I believe he indicated it was being undertaken jointly by his department and by the Department of Transport. I have found it extraordinarily difficult to obtain any information about these investigations. We cannot seem to find out whether an investigation has taken place on the site; we do not know whether any witnesses have been called, or whether any of the people interested have been questioned regarding the possibilities of this waterway. We do know, however, that the United States has undertaken a considerable study of its own part of the waterway, and I was disappointed, therefore, to learn that this government is showing so little interest in this matter if, indeed, it is showing any interest at all.
I think it is extremely important for Canada to know what the United States is contemplating and, in particular, what depth the authorities have in mind. It was suggested by the hon. member for St. James, if I understood him correctly, that the waterway would perhaps have a depth of 35 feet to New York. There may be something to be said in favour of such a waterway, but I have grave doubts whether the United States is contemplating anything of that nature. I understand that the channels to be used are, in the main, of such narrow width that in order to have such a depth sustaining walls would have to be built because of the erosion which would otherwise be caused by heavy waves. It is important that Canada should know what is being contemplated by the United States in order that we may be able to introduce continuity into the project and obtain the greatest degree of effectiveness from it.
Government spokesmen have said on many occasions in reply to questions which I have asked that investigations are going on, but I find it extremely strange that the government should not have called upon the international joint commission to resume the studies which were suspended in 1937. At that time, of the several possibilities which were offered it was stated that the most natural route was that which ran from lake Champlain to Sorel by way of the Richelieu river. That was said to be the most economical and feasible route, from an engineering point of view.
It was also stated in the report made at that time that it would be difficult for the international joint commission to make any definite recommendation until the St. Lawrence seaway had been completed. The seaway has been completed, and it seems to me that if the government really does wish to go ahead with this project the most practical thing to do would be to ask the international joint commission to resume the studies which were interrupted in 1937. Then we would also have the solution to the problem of fitting the project on the Canadian side into the project on the United States side so that we might have one complete waterway at the least possible expense.
I should like to bring to the attention of the government, and particularly to the Minister of Public Works-and I emphasize this very energetically-the fact that in 1937 the Department of Public Works did some work on the Richelieu river. They dug a 12-foot channel and built the locks at St. Louis to accommodate ships with a 12-foot draft. Work was also done on the dam at Fryer island with the view of having the St. Lawrence waterway run down through lake Champlain to Sorel. Because of the recommendations in the international joint commission report and because of the fact that the government has already spent a considerable amount of money in the preliminary work in this channel, I would suggest that before going on with any other project that might be contemplated the government might be wise indeed to complete the work that has already been started.
I should like the minister to make a special note of the last argument that I have advanced today and the fact that a good deal of work has been done on the Richelieu river up to St. John.
In view of the fact that the Richelieu waterway has a 12-foot draft, I would think it would be more practicable indeed to have this work completed at least to a 12-foot draft before any other work is undertaken.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks about a building project which is too much of a financial burden to taxpayers in Montreal island and in the town of St, Laurent, which I have the honour of representing in this house.
Now being built on Montreal island is the metropolitan boulevard as an answer to the traffic problems.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, the city of Montreal is known as the metropolis of Canada, and Montrealers are rightly proud of this. Montreal is the nerve centre not only of the province of Quebec but of all Canada. It is the railway and air centre of the country. It is also the highway centre of our country. That is why I feel that, if the Montreal metropolitan commission decided to build the metropolitan boulevard which crosses Montreal island from east to west and links with the Ottawa-Montreal and the Montreal-Quebec highways, the cost of this project should not fall solely on taxpayers within the island of Montreal, but our fellow citizens in the province of Quebec and in the whole country should also share that cost. Therefore, I think, like most people in the province of Quebec, that metropolitan boulevard should be part of the trans-Canada highway.
I realize that in recent years, under the Union Nationale administration headed by Mr. Duplessis, the province of Quebec invariably rejected the federal government's offer to contribute to the building of the trans-Canada highway and of metropolitan boulevard in Montreal.
Mr. Lesage promised to pay the entire cost.

After the death of Mr. Duplessis, Mr. Sauve became head of the province of Quebec. Being somewhat more broadminded in this respect, he indicated he was prepared to accept, to a certain extent, the contribution offered by the central government for the construction of the trans-Canada highway.
Since June 22 last, significant changes have occurred in the province of Quebec. We now have at the head of the government of that province the very man the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) just mentioned, the Hon. Mr. Jean Lesage, who stated in Montreal, last June 20, that he would do his utmost to settle the problem of Metropolitan boulevard.
He said the province would pay for the whole thing.

Precisely, he said the province would bear the whole cost for the construction of metropolitan boulevard. Now, for the information of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, who is so fond of interrupting his colleagues, let me read into the record the statement made by the Hon. Jean Lesage, on June 20, 1960, as reported in La Presse for June 21, 1960. Here it is:
A Liberal provincial government-
Such as we now have, my dear colleague.
A Liberal provincial government will bear the whole cost of construction and maintenance of the metropolitan boulevard.
Not only must the metropolitan boulevard be part of the provincial road network, but it must be a section of the trans-Canada highway.
A Liberal government in Quebec would therefore go to Ottawa and seek federal co-operation in the construction of that highway.
For ten years now I have been saying that we should accept money from Ottawa in that field.
It is money that belongs to us, since it came out of our taxes. We are prepared to complete the remaining section of the trans-Canada highway in the province. We will get Ottawa to pay half the cost of the work already done, and of the work which remains to be done.
That's fine.

Mr. Chairman, in the 1959 session, I put on the order paper a question asking whether the province of Quebec or the city of Montreal had asked the federal government to contribute towards the construction cost of the metropolitan boulevard.
The answer I got from the then minister of public works was in the negative.
Having read into the record that statement by Hon. Jean Lesage, I have no doubt
[Mr. Valade.l

that the Minister of Public Works will receive from the provincial government a request inviting him to contribute to the building costs of the trans-Canada highway in the province of Quebec, and I am convinced that authorities in the metropolis will ask him to participate in the construction of metropolitan boulevard in Montreal.
The Hon. Mr. Jean Lesage, premier of the province, has made a very definite statement on the matter. I trust that the present premier, ever anxious to preserve Quebec's provincial rights, will be prepared to start negotiations with the federal authorities and to co-operate with them, though always in keeping with the rights of the province and of the citizens of the province of Quebec.
Right now, as I have just said, this is far too heavy a burden for Montreal taxpayers. So much so that, only a few months ago, every taxpayer got a special tax bill at the rate of 13J per cent of his assessment, to pay for the cost of metropolitan boulevard.
I therefore ask the minister, jointly with the present premier of Quebec, to relieve Montreal taxpayers. I hope that, in fairness to the people of Montreal, the Minister of Public Works will co-operate with Quebec provincial authorities.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal very briefly with a problem which more particularly affects my fellow citizens of St. Laurent. In 1957, the government and the then minister of public works authorized the building of a post office in St. Laurent. Before the construction work started on the new post office, the first sod had been turned by the present hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) who had taken an active part in the development of that project in St. Laurent. the mayor of St. Laurent for the construe- . tion of new buildings, new post offices in the constituency of Dollard. In each case, the reply was negative.
I do not think the building of two new post offices in the constituency of Dollard is an immediate necessity. The previous administration had built fine post offices in Youville and also in St. Laurent. Moreover, when the new post office was built at St. Laurent, provision was made for the addition of another floor to accommodate a new unemployment insurance office and even a new customs office, which would have been most convenient for several hundreds of industries and thousands of workers. As I understand it, there are thousands of unemployed under the present government, despite its promises that there would be no unemployment if it was elected to office. I hardly think the premier of the province of Quebec needs the advice of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), an exsecretary of the former premier, to guide the destinies of the province of Quebec.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I ask the present Minister of Public Works to consult with his colleagues, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and discuss the advisability of adding a floor to the present post office in St. Laurent, to accommodate an unemployment insurance office and a customs office, which would be of great convenience to hundreds of industries located in that part of Montreal island.

speechtext:
I have no desire, Mr. Chair -mon, to delay the passage of these estimates by even a short and qualified eulogy of the minister. However, I should like to say a few
6596	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works words in a general way as the member for Algoma East. In that capacity I do want to acknowledge the fact that the minister and his officials have always dealt with any request I have made of them in the field of public works, both courteously and expeditiously. We are now discussing the first item in public works, and the discussion has ranged far and wide over general and detailed considerations. Perhaps the most important general consideration has been the fact that the amount to be appropriated for public works this year is many millions of dollars less than previously, although we were informed that a great public works program was the main plank in the government's platform for dealing with unemployment. I will not say anything more about that. My hon. friend, who opened the discussion for our side dealt with it and I thought very effectively.
However, if there is any part of Canada at the present time where some governmental action in connection with unemployment is required, in the field of public works or any other field, that place is in my own constituency at Elliot Lake. I should like to say a word or two about that situation and what might or might not be done by the Department of Public Works. There certainly is a need for employment, and whether that need can be met by public works or in any other way, the need is becoming increasingly serious. So far, either in this field or in any other field, all we have heard from the government is that a committee is still considering the matter. I believe a committee was considering the matter last November.
In the estimates there is an amount for a federal building at Elliot Lake. I take it, though the minister when he replies may correct me, that there has been no change in the plans to proceed with that building. When the appropriation was first made for this building in Elliot Lake I applauded the decision to go ahead with it as one who had been advocating such a building for some time. My advocacy of this building was on the assumption, which I thought was a reasonable one, that the work the building would have to do and the services it would have to render would be those which we had in mind when the building was first considered and when the government decided to go ahead with it. In other words. I assumed it would be a federal building to serve a community of between 25,000 and 30,000 people.
It is an interesting commentary on the statement which has been made by representatives of the government that we should 

have known years ago how insecure the economic foundation for Elliot Lake was, to find that the plans for this building made only a year or so ago were based on a community of this size. In other words at that time, a year or so ago, before the decision made in Washington, apparently it was contemplated by the government that the building would be required to service the community that had been envisaged previously when it looked as if the United States government would take up the option. Perhaps the minister will tell the committee in due course, in replying to the multitudinous questions with which he will be dealing, what changes if any have been required in this federal building.
There is something else that can be done in the field of public works to assist this hard-pressed community and that is the construction of a dock at Cutler on Georgian bay close to where the road from Elliot Lake meets the highway. I am sure the minister knows about this proposal for a dock in this area where there is a first class deep-water harbour suitable for ships of any draught. The proposal for this dock was made some years ago when the previous government was in office. It was made at that time primarily as a means of assisting the development of Elliot Lake. As the minister perhaps knows, and if he does not I am sure the deputy minister knows, there were long and complicated negotiations between the minister of public works of that day, the uranium mining industry and a coal importing corporation. These negotiations were aimed at making arrangements by which the cost of this dock, which would have been considerable, could have been shared between the government, the mining industry and this coal company. A great deal of progress was made in bringing these negotiations to a head, and in 1957 it looked as if we might be successful. At that time the negotiations broke down and there has been no progress made in recent years.
It is quite easy to understand why the negotiations broke down. During the election campaign of 1957 the present Prime Minister, in his short tour through my constituency, promised that the dock would be built at that place at the expense of the government. Once that promise was made and once the leader of the party making that promise became the Prime Minister there was little likelihood of any private agency

making a contribution to the cost of a dock which the Prime Minister had promised at government expense. However, apparently this idea has been revived in recent months because of the exigencies of the employment situation at Elliot Lake and along the north shore. There is no doubt that a dock of this kind would be of assistance in the industrial development of this whole area. I should like to ask the minister what progress, if any, has been made in this proposal for a dock, in the light of some press reports that have been brought to my attention. I have before me a report from the Toronto Globe and Mail. It is from its Ottawa correspondent and is dated July 12 and in it he says this:
It was learned today-
That is July 12.
-that the federal government plans to encourage at Cutler, site of a plant which manufactures hydrochloric acid for the uranium mines.
That is the government plans construction at Cutler of this dock.
The plant, with a small dock of its own, is located at the foot of a large bay on the north shore of lake Huron. The area already is served by the Trans-Canada highway and a railway line.
I should like to know whether in fact the government does plan any such construction because of the importance of this matter to Elliot Lake and to the whole area concerned. In view of the industrial situation there and the situation of the uranium mining industry it is more important than ever before. This report has raised in the minds of the people in that area great hopes which are not unconnected with the realization that there was another specific assurance made by the Prime Minister that this dock would be built by the government, an assurance which I have stated was made in 1957. Presumably it is one of those assurances which, as the Minister of Transport has told us so often, when the Prime Minister makes it, it means that it is to be kept.
The other day there was in Ottawa a representative of the Elliot Lake chamber of commerce or the Elliot Lake administration because it is not a municipality, Mr. Robert Hart, chairman of the board of trustees. When he returned to Elliot Lake-it was last week some time

he reported to the Elliot Lake Standard as follows:
Mr. Hart said yesterday that the main reason for his trip to Ottawa had been to press for assurances from the government that some announcement would be forthcoming before the end of the present session of parliament.

That announcement would concern assistance of the government to the community which has been promised. Mr. Hart went on to say this, as quoted in this paper:
From my talks with Mr. Churchill and Mr. Thrasher it seems there is definite hope the government's proposals for a dock at Cutler ... are coming to a head.
There are two reports, then one in the Globe and Mail and one in the Elliot Lake Standard, that the government is to construct this dock, a dock which I have said would mean so much to that hard pressed community at this time. When the minister replies I hope he will be able to tell us that this matter has indeed come to a head and that this dock will be proceeded with; although I have been unable to find any indication that there is an appropriation for this dock in the estimates. That is all I wish to bring to the attention of the committee at this time, Mr. Chairman, although I will have something to say about the detailed items in the estimates when we reach them.

The estimates of the Department of Public Works are a matter which is always of interest to my riding, even as they are to the ridings of most hon. members. However, my riding of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador has some problems which, if

Supply-Public Works not altogether peculiar to it, certainly are much greater than those existing in some other ridings.
In central Newfoundland transportation is of great importance and also the completion of the trans-Canada highway. The Grand Falls area and the towns adjacent to it depend completely on land transportation. Their newest port is Lewisporte. The completion of the trans-Canada highway is of great importance to it. Although the provincial government has carried out an extensive road building program since Newfoundland entered confederation, nevertheless the cost of the trans-Canada highway is a grievous one. I am not alone in thinking that the cost of the trans-Canada highway which comes under the minister's department not only in Newfoundland but in the Atlantic provinces should be borne, at least to the extent of 90 per cent, by the federal government. The federal government is really the only agency which can provide adequate road transportation in Newfoundland and in fact in the four Atlantic provinces.
It is generally admitted that transportation is one of the great problems. Transportation needs are extremely important in the Atlantic provinces. Perhaps I might point out that both parties seem to agree on this matter. Part of the declared policy of the Liberal party in early 1958 was to help remove the economic disabilities of the Atlantic provinces and to advocate special assistance for the provision of trunk highways in all four Atlantic provinces where heavy traffic to and from central Canada all focus and to promote opportunity for the tourist industry. The Progressive Conservative party in the Atlantic resolutions promised adjustment in freight rates and the provision of transportation facilities in order to allow our producers reasonable access to the markets of Canada. There is perhaps no better way in which some of the disadvantages of geography in the Atlantic provinces can be offset than by the building of federal highways, not only the trans-Canada highway but federal trunk roads connecting with it.
To return to my own riding of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, may I say that such roads as the road from the trans-Canada highway to Lewisporte should, in my opinion, be a federal highway. I think the trans-Canada highway itself should be considered mostly as a federal responsibility. These trunk highways can, to some degree at least, offset the disadvantages from which the Atlantic provinces suffer owing to geography and, may I add, high freight rates.
Small wharves and breakwaters have a value far in excess of the dollars and cents [Mr. Granger.!
which they cost. I will not weary the committee by repeating my argument about the growing importance of fisheries in Newfoundland and the growing importance, I should like to say, of the fisheries in northern Newfoundland and Labrador, in order to keep it in my own riding.
The fact is that the northern fishery is becoming more important not only to Newfoundland itself but also to the fish plants in Nova Scotia. All have an interest in the development of the Labrador fishery. These small works, such as breakwaters, slipways for handling small boats and small wharves which serve as a community fishery centre, have greater importance by far than they appear to from their cost in dollars and cents. They contribute to greater efficiency and to making the fisherman's lot a little easier and better and his production of fish a little greater. In that sense their importance is very great indeed.
Therefore I would ask the minister to look very carefully into the various requests which have been made from time to time for these small works, these small slipways, wharves and breakwaters which are needed throughout northern Newfoundland, in the straits of Belle Isle and along the coast of Labrador. Certainly if there is any thought given to a larger program of public works I would hope they would be included in such program.
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo mentioned the fact that he hoped the cost of the St. John's harbour would not mean a reduction in spending in other parts of Newfoundland. I would like to associate myself with what he said, and I think his meaning was clear.
As far as I am concerned, although St. John's is not in my riding I do feel that the man who owns a schooner in White Bay has a definite interest in work done in St. John's. Those engaged in coastal trade, regardless of the part of Newfoundland from which they come, have an interest in the developments taking place in the harbour at St. John's, because as a result of these harbour developments their problems should ease somewhat. They could get a quicker and more efficient turn-around when their ships enter St. John's. I do not think any of them would in any way wish to criticize developments taking place in St. John's which to some extent would have a beneficial effect on all of Newfoundland.
However, I would hate to see any reduction in the spending on these small works which I mentioned in fishing communities where the primary producer must depend on them in order to do the work properly and efficiently. As I said, I will not give any names place

by place where these works are needed. I have written from time to time to the minister and I am sure they are given consideration as I send them in. I would hope that when a new program is announced these places in remote areas will not be forgotten.
I would also like to mention one or two larger works which are needed at places like Baie Verte and Botwood, where this is a perennial request. I again make my annual plea on behalf of Botwood, and I also ask for some adequate wharf facilities at Lewis-porte. These places are very important centres of trade and I hope to see them included in the coming year's projects. Baie Verte is likely to be the centre of a large mining development and it badly needs something in the nature of a wharf.
Then if I may continue with my annual requests in the matter of public buildings, Happy Valley certainly should have a post office building. At Glenwood there used to be a public building there in the old days of responsible government in Newfoundland, and the town badly needs a post office building. In putting up these public buildings I again emphasize that they are monuments to Canada and should be treated as such. Properly designed buildings which bear the name of Canada are the best advertisement that we belong to a modern, advancing nation. I think the minister and his department should keep in mind that the more of these buildings which go up the stronger will be our ties.
I would like to review for a moment, before I conclude my brief remarks, the importance of the trans-Canada highway and ask the minister to look carefully into the possibility of the federal government building the trans-Canada highway and trunk roads in Newfoundland, in Labrador and in the Atlantic provinces. Because of their geographic handicap and the shifting of trade further into more prosperous central parts of Canada, as well as their great transportation problems, there has been, if I might use the word, a deconfederated tendency. One way to offset that, as I said before, and perhaps the best way national unity can be improved and advanced is to improve transportation. There is no better way in this modern age, until everyone uses jet planes for transportation, than to build federal highways.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to spend a few minutes on the estimates of the minister's department because, as has been stated here today, no other department is of such importance to our region in general than the Department of Public Works.
Supply-Public Works
I should like to support the comments made by hon. members opposite from Newfoundland with respect to the proportion of the expenditure of the minister's estimates for the St. John's harbour development. Whilst no one will argue that there is no more important public works projects in our province than the development of St. John's harbour, there are nevertheless public works of a nature that are of importance to the fishery and the general economy of that part of Canada.
There is a tendency, I am sure quite a natural one, in viewing the over-all picture to look at the votes of the minister's department and note that more than half of the total vote is going into the St. John's harbour development this year and I think that should constantly be borne in mind. We do not for a moment suggest that the development of this important harbour should be at the expense of other equally important projects in other parts of the country. I have in my own constituency projects which could be of a substantial nature which I believe are not being given the attention they deserve because of the tremendous expenditure which has been currently undertaken in connection with the development of St. John's harbour. Breakwaters are very expensive projects with very high labour content, extremely important to navigation and to the trade and commerce of our area.
In my own riding I can give you two projects of a substantial size in connection with breakwater construction which should be considered in the minister's estimates next year. I wish to refer to the necessity of providing a breakwater to the beach at Bell island. This breakwater is necessary so that maximum public benefit may be obtained from the public warehouse which the minister had the privilege of officially opening, and it is also necessary in the context of the new Belle island ferry which is soon to go into operation. Soundings have been taken, surveys have been made and all that is needed now is the minister's approval. I hope that when he replies at the end of this estimate he will have some favourable word to say which will lead us to believe that this project will be considered in next year's estimates.
With the change in defence expenditure- and I am thinking now of the curtailment of the United States defence expenditure in eastern Newfoundland-there has resulted a general rejuvenation of the shore fishing. Many of us believe this to be a good thing, because we feel that revenue from fishing is much more stable and consequently more beneficial to the economy in the long run than defence expenditures. In connection with this revitalization of the shore fishing-hundreds

Supply-Public Works of our men are returning to it-there are many functions which the minister's department could perform which would be of tremendous benefit.
I am thinking of small slipways, small fishermen's wharves and, of course, of not so small breakwaters which are necessary in order to provide safe and adequate shelter. At the eastermost end of St. John's and towards the cape St. Francis area there are many places where breakwaters are needed.
I could give a long list of such cases, but I will refrain from doing so now. I would ask the minister to take into consideration when he is reviewing these various projects for the coming year that these works are very necessary and should be carried out with all due dispatch because of the employment which could be derived from them and, more important still, because of the shot in the arm it would give the fisheries in Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am prompted to rise again not only because I have been requested to do so by those on behalf of whom I intend to speak but also because of the similarity between the situation at Elliot Lake of which the Leader of the Opposition has spoken and the community about which I desire to speak at the moment.
I have referred to the team which the minister has appointed in co-operation with the Minister of Transport to consider port facilities all along the St. Lawrence, its north shore, its south shore and also from Dorion in Quebec to Oshawa just outside the city of Toronto. I have no intention of going over the material which I placed before the committee on an earlier occasion, but I must tell the minister with all respect, and I am sure he will take it in this light, that I do not think very much of the team which he and the Minister of Transport have established to deal with a matter of this nature.
I will tell the hon. gentleman why. The first reason is that the experts who compose this team exclude anyone from a crown corporation known as the St. Lawrence seaway authority. Here is a team from two departments which seeks to come to the assistance of ports along the seaway and which gives no consideration whatsoever to those who know more about the seaway than does either the Department of Public Works or the Department of Transport. There has been established a crown corporation and within that corporation there is a statistician, an economist and a number of other people who know a great deal about the seaway. How then is it possible to give the consideration which is required with regard to the establishment of secondary industry or with regard to future development unless there is on the team someone who has the figures, the

statistics, and who is in a position to assist the team with regard to the other laudable objective which the team has in mind?
Now, as I have said before, this example is not being followed elsewhere. I think that in order that this team may consider properly the requirements in the province of Quebec at Seven Islands, at Pointe Noire, which is,
I believe, the port that is being established as a result of the new bill which was introduced into the house the other day, the Wabush railway bill; at Sorel, at Baie Comeau, at Contrecoeur, at Rimouski and at many other ports to which, I am sure, the team must have given consideration-there are 29 of them, as I remember-it is not sufficient to consider these ports in themselves.
It is essential that the over-all picture be considered. In this connection it is important that one of the finest reports ever made on the St. Lawrence seaway be kept in mind. I refer to the study made by the University of Indiana in conjunction with the Chicago board of trade concerning grain movements. It is important that the impact of the seaway on the Montreal area within a radius of 100 miles, the subject of a study by McGill University and the Montreal research council be considered. It is important that the reports of the Canadian National Railways be considered. It is important that the report established and made public by the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation-the United States entity-be given consideration.
What is being done by this team of experts from the two departments I have mentioned is hard to ascertain, because when I moved to obtain from the minister the plans that this team had prepared for the various ports under consideration, that motion was turned down.
Secret reports.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like now to bring to the attention of the minister, and then send across to him, provided he will give it back to me, a study which has been made by the New York Central railroad system of industrial sites, and I commend this to the hon. gentleman's attention and to the attention of the team which he and the Department of Transport have established. This is a consideration of the seven sites upon which industry can be established on the United States side of the boundary line extending from the international line at St. Regis, which we discussed when we were considering the pilotage bill the other day, right to the foot of lake Ontario. It is a most complete report which contains a map of each community, a map of the industrial sites in each community and references to railroads, labour conditions, available power supplies and the like.

At the end of this booklet is an over-all description of the effect of the St. Lawrence seaway on northern New York state, most of which information has been taken from the public report prepared by the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation, the United States entity, in connection with these ports. I would ask the minister to look at that and see if the team that he has in mind is giving the kind of consideration to the 29 areas, most of them in the province of Quebec, many of them in eastern Ontario, that are being considered.
When I rose I said that I had been asked to bring a matter to the attention of the minister arising out of the report of the team, and which makes it akin to Elliot Lake. I refer, of course, to the very serious position in which the city of Cornwall is at the present time. I quote from an article appearing in the Standard-Freeholder, dated April 16, 1960:
For nearly three quarters of a century, Cornwall's progress was linked with the cotton textile industry. The cotton business had its ups and downs, but it grew until it became a major factor in the community's economy.
Now there is no longer a cotton textile industry in Cornwall, and over the past few years it has cost about 2,400 people their jobs. The decline has been even more rapid in the past six or eight months.
I should have said the article is entitled:
