Elliot Lake and Cornwall have something in common.
However, the government has seen fit, in conjunction with the provincial government of Ontario, to do something for the community of Elliot Lake. Of course I am not complaining about that; on the contrary I commend both governments for what they can or may do on behalf of that stricken community, but I should like to draw to the attention of the minister and of the team that has gone to that community what is being done by Cornwall Industrial Developments Limited, a non-profit corporation, to assist industry and the team in the development of that area. May I read just one short paragraph from a memorandum of Cornwall Industrial Developments Limited. It reads:
Since the completion of the hydro project and the closing of the cotton industries, Cornwall has had to face a heavy unemployment situation and, as a result, larger city relief bills. The C.I.D.L. ever aware of this situation, has left no stone unturned to find a solution. They have sent delegations to cities in the United States of America with similar distressed areas where vacant factories were purchased by a citizens' company, leased or resold, with the result that many new smaller Industries were established employing hundreds of people.
This C.I.D.L. is composed of a group of local citizens, a non-profit operating group, who have purchased all of the bulidings
Supply-Public Works owned by the Canadian cotton mills for a substantial sum of money. Their worthwhile objects are:
1.	To examine all industrial opportunities regardless of size which need special help.
2.	Make preliminary studies and analysis of the proposals.
3.	Arrange meetings with the parties who would be interested in the specific type of proposal: banks, insurance companies, investment dealers, and so forth.
4.	Supply the required equity capital provided the required investigations indicate the feasibility of the project.
5.	Assist in every way possible the industrial expansion program of the city.
I now come to the team. The team went to Cornwall, and after having looked over the situation hurriedly, decided in favour of assisting the community by the construction of docks at the west end of the community. This is all to the good. They did not at the time-again I say this with deference-take the trouble to look to the front of the city. If they had they would have seen that there were already established, or about to be established, by the Department of Transport through the St. Lawrence seaway authority, 27-foot facilities. Having done that, they made a recommendation which, of course, was accepted gratefully by the community. Later on it became evident that perhaps the site which they had selected was questionable, so down they went again and this time they discovered that right in front of the city of Cornwall there was a dock which needed an extension of some 500 feet and with the extension of 500 feet would be right on 27-foot facilities, thus enabling secondary industry to be established in the area.
I hold a picture of the dock in my hand. It happens to be in front of three large cotton factories which employed as many as 2,400 men and which are now completely closed down. This is the property which has been bought by C.I.D.L. They wish to encourage secondary industry to come to that area.
My regret is that several months ago this was not discovered by the team of the minister because any person who knows anything about what is going on-and I am sure the Minister of Transport did, as well as the seaway authority-could have told the team that went down there that instead of spending now large sums of money in the area which they had in mind at the time, by the simple extension of the wharf opposite this area, and other facilities that I am going to bring to the attention of the minister now, it would have been possible to come more quickly to the assistance of this stricken community.

Supply-Public Works
One final word: in the estimates of the Department of Transport there is a sum of $50,000 for the extension of this wharf. I want to make a special appeal to the minister and say to him that this is not enough. Here is a group of local citizens who are putting their own money into a corporation, not for profit, not in order to make any money themselves but in order to encourage industry, as the New York Central booklet which I sent across to the Minister of Public Works is doing, and they are going to send to many thousands of people in Canada and outside of Canada copies of the booklet which indicates what is being done. The sum of $50,000, therefore, is not enough. This community needs far more than that. I appeal to the minister to do more. What can he do? Over and above the extension of the wharf I think he can assist in the construction of a hangar; I think he can assist particularly with reference to secondary industry because surely that must be the object of the team. Surely it must be the intention of this team to profit by the seaway development into which Canada has put large sums of money in order to attract secondary industry to this country.
I read in the press that the government has established an interdepartmental committee, the object of which is to consider ways and means, by the establishment of a fund of some $200 million and, by the way, by a reduction in taxation, to assist industry to come to these areas. That is all to the good. In what way is the team established by the two departments working in co-operation with the interdepartmental committee?
Unless and until this team has considered these various reports and the over-all aspect of this international project upon various parts of Canada, in my opinion it will not be able to do the job that it should do. Why do I say that? I say that because what is the use of spending large sums of money in an area unless it is known, because of an over-all study of the project, where traffic is likely to go. The University of Indiana study, in conjunction with the Chicago board of trade, has come to the conclusion that Baie Comeau and one or two or other ports on the north shore of the St. Lawrence are going to benefit tremendously by the movement of grain. The McGill report, in conjunction with an advisory committee of the city of Montreal, has come to the conclusion that certain movements of grain will benefit Montreal whereas other movements are likely to hurt it. Thus far the results have been most favourable to the city of Montreal. But I say that if you consider a particular project without having regard to the overall picture you cannot come to a proper and logical conclusion.

I take my seat with this appeal to the minister. If we are going to deal with the serious unemployment situation that affects Canada as a whole, but particular areas more seriously than others-the one I have mentioned is, of course, a particular one that has suffered in an especial manner-I think the team could do a far better job if, over and above the physical conditions that are required in the area, consideration could be given by the team to the over-all aspect and to secondary industry. I appeal to the minister and ask him if he will not give consideration to a substantial increase in the expenditure of money which this community has requested of his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if there are other members who wish to speak on the first item I certainly will yield.

Just before the minister
speaks, I trust that he has given consideration to the questions I asked on Monday and again today. It would be very unfortunate if answers should first appear in the newspapers during the week. We have already had an article in the newspapers today which answers in part one of my questions. In justice to his department and his officers I think the minister should tell the committee who asked for these works at Malartic and Duparquet and who recommended them, and also answer the other questions I have put to him. They are very simple questions requiring only short answers and I think the minister should do that in his reply.

If there is no one else who wishes to speak before the minister replies, I should like to join in what has been said by all members from Newfoundland, with the exception, of course, of the minister who obviously could not say this though I imagine he agrees with the rest of us, as to our hope that the very large sums of money being expended in St. John's harbour, as a result of the initiative taken by Mr. Winters when he was minister in getting the study started, will not prejudice the minister or treasury board with respect to the rest of Newfoundland. There is in Newfoundland, for reasons which I do not need to repeat, a need for works as great as in any other part of Canada. So far as the rivers and harbours vote is concerned, Newfoundland has enjoyed for a short time the benefits of much heavier public expenditures which the rest of Canada has enjoyed for the greater part of the period since 1867, as the minister himself very justly recognized when he appeared on television in Newfoundland and made certain observations which were much appreciated and which excited great hopes there. I hope the minister will make sure

those hopes are not dashed by treasury board.
I am sure that when the minister made those statements he meant them and meant to carry them out.
I should also like to ask the minister if he as a new minister would try to do something which we were not able to get his predecessor to do and do not seem to be able to get the Postmaster General to do, that is, to get rid of this ossification of the mind about post offices in Newfoundland. The whole history of the post office in Newfoundland for historical reasons is quite different from the post office on the mainland of Canada. I say this as someone who had considerable experience at one time with rural life in one old province of Canada and who has spent a good many months in the outports of Newfoundland.
In many places in the rest of Canada it is a custom acceptable to the communities to have small post offices in country stores. The idea that the post office should be an adjunct to something else and that the income should be an adjunct to other income is quite acceptable to everybody in the community. For historical reasons, and I am sure the minister from Newfoundland will bear me out in this, in the outports of Newfoundland this would be an entirely unacceptable situation. It is for that reason that in many places in Newfoundland where the postal income is away below what it is elsewhere in Canada post offices did exist under the old commission government.
Since confederation it has been the custom for the Department of Public Works under the previous and present governments to replace these buildings rather reluctantly when they became totally obsolete, when the roofs started to leak and the buildings started to fall down. I wish the minister could get rid of some of that reluctance. I wish he could also get rid of the silly idea that if there was a post office before confederation there is some sort of inherent right to have one now but that if a community has grown since confederation and has become bigger than many of these other places it should be excluded because the growth was more recent. I am counting on the minister from Newfoundland to do something about this matter and exert some influence on the government because this is something with respect to which I think the present government and the present minister could attain a great deal of credit for themselves if they would make a change.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
May I reply first to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and tell him that personally I know of no people
Supply-Public Works in Canada whom I admire and like more than the Newfoundlanders, and they know that very well. As a consequence I have a particular proclivity for allowing many things to Newfoundland which otherwise might come under certain criticism. I think it is correct to say that Newfoundland deserves everything she is getting and at the present time no other province can compare on a per capita basis with Newfoundland, so far as capital expenditures by the Department of Public Works are concerned. Such expenditures are far greater per capita than in any other province. I hope that for some time to come that may be so because Newfoundland is in great need of public works. It is my hope that as long as I am minister Newfoundland will get them.
I am constantly importuned by the minister from Newfoundland, also by the youngest member of the house, the hon. member for St. John's East, and also, I must say, by members on the opposite side, for whom I have great respect, as to the needs of Newfoundland.
You do not get more than one letter a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Well, that is pretty good, but it does not compare with the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg who, since I became minister on August 1, has sent me 383 letters. I received the last one today.
Does he ever do anything else?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I think it is to his credit. He does not speak too often in the house, and I do not know that that can be said about everyone. I am not referring to anyone in particular, now.
This has been a very pleasant day for me, and one from which I have derived a great deal of benefit. I am not going to try to answer in detail all these questions at the moment because as consideration of the estimates continues I hope to raise certain points. However, in deference to the Leader of the Opposition, I believe I should reply to him first. He asked me about the federal building at Elliot Lake. It is quite true that it was planned for a thriving community when the uranium industry was at the height of its development. Now, as a result of the misfortunes which have overtaken that community, through no fault of its own, I was importuned to cut back substantially on that federal building. The best I would agree to do was to take off one storey. It is still going to be a substantial building of two storeys instead of three. Believe me, Elliot Lake
6604	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works needs that because the building is going to house many of the departments of government.
In so far as the dock at Cutler is concerned, I want to start out by telling hon. members that this dock at Cutler was consistently refused by a former minister of public works, the Hon. Robert Winters. This was, of course, before he became the president of a great uranium industry up there. He consistently refused the dock at a time when activities at Elliot Lake were booming, when the uranium industry was at its height. He insisted, and one can see merit in the argument, that there should be amortization payments over a period of years by means of which the government would get back the money it put into the dock. When these guaranteed payments were not forthcoming the minister, in his wisdom, refused this dock.
I have no hesitation in saying that the situation has changed. The industries in Elliot Lake are not booming. If the building of a dock at Cutler would substantially improve the situation in Elliot Lake, and only if it would, the government might be willing to build this dock. There is no purpose served by building a dock unless there are going to be industries to use it, and use it adequately. I do not mind saying that during the past weeks and months I have as minister been negotiating with a certain company and urging that company to build a manufacturing plant at Cutler. This would provide employment up there. It was my hope that perhaps we could have an affirmative answer from this company. Of course, the company has its problems. It has to know whether it could market the product it contemplates manufacturing and whether the venture would be successful. This company has seen the Ontario government to ascertain what considerations could be obtained from that source.
Until I hear from that great, public-spirited company, I am unable to come to any conclusion about building a dock at Cutler. As you know, Mr. Chairman, and as the members of the committee will appreciate, we cannot just build docks because people are in a difficult situation-
Or because the Prime Minister promised them.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
-unless they are going to be of material benefit to make the expenditure worth while. The situation has changed tremendously since 1957 when the dock was refused by the former government. Before we build a dock we must see that over a period of years the payments will amortize the cost of that dock, even although the period of years might be greatly extended beyond any 

ordinary arrangements made in regard to wharves or docks and this arrangement we will make with any new industry.
I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that this matter, as well as every other suggestion that has ever come to me in connection with Elliot Lake has received, and will receive, my most profound attention. I think I can say that that applies to every other minister of the government. I have never seen a committee more devoted to the problems of a community than the committee on Elliot Lake. This is a very difficult problem for which to find a solution. The problem was certainly not created by us but it is one for which we feel a very real responsibility to try to assuage the depressed condition with which this community is faced at the present time. If and when there is any news from this corporation which contemplates building this industry there, if we can come to any decision, I would be happy to make the announcement to the house and particularly to my friend the Leader of the Opposition who I know is very interested in this.
May I speak now for a moment concerning the request of the hon. member for Laurier. He referred to the departmental committee, of which I was very proud as I thought everyone was, set up by the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works in connection with harbour and port facilities along the St. Lawrence. I was surprised to hear the hon. member's criticisms because the committee has been highly praised from all sides. May I say that I feel his suggestion that this interdepartmental committee should consult with the St. Lawrence seaway authority is an excellent one. He will be very happy to hear that Mr. Manning, who is a great authority himself and a member of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, is the committee's liaison and is in constant touch with this interdepartmental committee, making available to the committee all relevant information. The desire of the hon. member for Laurier is, therefore, already an accomplished fact.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Yes, certainly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the minister not think there should be on the committee a representative of the St. Lawrence seaway authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I think there is a lot of merit in what the hon. member for Laurier suggests. I am going to give that most careful consideration, and I would be glad to discuss it with the Minister of Transport.

Then I noticed this brochure, which is very helpful. I usually hold on to most things that come into my hands but because the hon. member has requested its return, I shall return it. This brochure has been published, not by the United States authority corresponding to the St. Lawrence seaway authority but I understand by the government of the state of New York through the auspices of the New York Central railroad system. This is an excellent brochure and gives us some very good ideas that may be very helpful.
May I also congratulate the hon. member for Laurier on his continuing interest in his old riding of Stormont, and upon what he has said about Cornwall. I do not know of any member who exhibits the zeal of the present member for Stormont in the interests of Cornwall. I believe he is in to see me or the Minister of Transport at least once a week concerning the problems of Cornwall and about the very pressing problem of a wharf or dock.
The information given me today by the hon. member for Laurier is quite correct. The dock that he indicated is now available. Of course, as he knows so well, it was not available earlier when our team went down there the first time. However, I can assure him that the plight of Cornwall is very much in our minds and will be given every consideration.
In reply to the hon. member for Levis, may I say that I did not know that his question needed a reply. I thought perhaps he was joking when he said that in connection with the Prince Edward Island causeway, "we were given the brush-off". I do not know what he means by "brush-off". The work we have done investigating the Prince Edward Island causeway has been tremendous. It has been so extensive, this study that we have made to ascertain whether such a causeway is feasible under all the circumstances; it is as great a study as has ever been made on an enterprise of this kind. Because of its uniqueness and because it is the first time that any such study has been really gone through to the extreme limit, the first time in the world such a causeway has been studied to such a degree, I was of the opinion that the hon. member for Levis would feel, as do most of the other members of the house, that we have really done this thoroughly. We have done this job thoroughly and well. Unless it should be said that I was guilty-

I am sorry to interrupt the minister but will he tell me what information is needed for his department to estimate the cost of the causeway? When I spoke two days ago I gave him a list. I took that list from a report that was made by the deputy
Supply-Public Works when he went down to investigate all of the work that was done there. Of course, I am not an engineer; I am no expert. But I feel that with the information the department already has they can certainly estimate the cost of the project. I, therefore, want to tell the minister that I was not joking at all; far from it. I took this information from the report which I read very carefully. In addition to that, the minister will also recall that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate once asked him a question to the effect that the minister had stated that the price of $400 million was very much too high. If the minister was capable at that time of saying that the cost of $400 million was too high, may I ask on what basis he was saying that amount was too high?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In reply to the hon. member for Levis may I say I was basing that reply on just plain, ordinary, good, old fashioned common sense of which the hon. member for Levis has a good deal.
In other words, it is just a guess.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: A guess as to $400 million being too much? Oh, no. Surely the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, himself an outstanding yachtsman and great authority on bridges, would not say that. No, no, that is not correct. In reply to the hon. member for Levis-and I am being very serious-may I say that until we receive from the national research council the results of this investigation into currents and other local phenomena or the effect of the causeway on this area, we are not in a position even to hazard a guess. As the hon. member who was himself parliamentary assistant to the minister of public works knows, these are extremely intricate studies. However, I can assure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that it will not be $400 million. If we had thought it was going to cost that much, we would have stopped this research long ago.
What is the minister's ceiling?
Five feet eight inches.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I was going to reply to the hon. member for Kootenay West but I think he has made such a lucid explanation of the combination of lover's walk and operation lemon juice-I do not know whether or not there was any analogy between the two-that I do not think it is necessary. I think the explanation he has given fairly well resolves itself into the necessity for me to say nothing except that the lover's walk was ordered closed many years ago by the former government. As a matter of fact I think the late
6606	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King himself confirmed that closing and he himself was a very romantic person in his conception of nature. He himself suggested that it should be closed, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police all along have insisted that it should remain closed because it is extremely dangerous.
To whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I mean dangerous, not in the way in which the hon. member for Kootenay West is thinking-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: -but dangerous to life and limb. Anybody that goes out there is apt to have a serious accident; I mean a physical accident.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
You are apt to slip and fall. Just recently, as a matter of fact, a man was very badly hurt.
For what he has said I want to thank the hon. member for Villeneuve who I always knew to be a courteous gentleman.
I was dumbfounded after the debate on Monday night to find the next day when I got home my neighbours on Revelstoke would not speak to me as I paddled up in my canoe and my wife also looked at me amiss because the headlines in the paper that night was this "Accuse Walker of patronage and payroll padding". That was quite a charge. You can appreciate that even a person's wife is shocked to see a statement of that kind. I am glad to note today that the newspaper which inadvertently carried that headline has corrected it. But what a bewildering thing it is to get into public life innocently, to come down here to do the best one can and because you refuse to be guilty of patronage you are accused of patronage. This morning I am damned because I gave the contract to the low bidder. On Monday night I was damned because I did not give it to the low bid, because of inefficiency. It is a terrible combination. How can I win gentlemen, I ask you?
On the question of payroll padding may I say this? If I through the greatest stretch of anyone's imagination can have any responsibility for this-and of course the hon. member for Villeneuve has made it quite clear that I have not-the suggestions that one sees from time to time are enough to shock one. If one did not have 55 years of reputation, one would begin to wonder what would happen to one's reputation when one becomes a minister of the crown in almost any government. In any event, it has been quite a novel experience for me. I am glad I am not as thin


skinned as are some people or you could appreciate that these things would really make one wonder.
I want to thank the hon. member for his co-operation and for his understanding that we cannot disclose information. I do not suppose it would be terrible but when a prosecution is contemplated it is a great thing for the government, the police and all the investigating authorities to keep their mouths shut and to get on with the investigation, and, if called for, prosecution.
As was done in the railway committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
-so as not to disclose any information that might be of benefit to any possible defendant in a criminal action. But I am glad to answer the question asked by the hon. member for Villeneuve and he said he would settle for that.
I am referring now to Malartic. I just received this information from the department. I have hardly had a chance to read it and I will read the answer as it was written. Routine inspection by departmental engineers showed that the wharf was in disrepair and a hazard to the public. The wharf was constructed in 1935 and very little maintenance had been done since that time. An estimate of the cost of repairs was submitted to the department. The work was approved on April 24, 1959.
As to Duparquet lake, that involves the cleaning of the rivers there. The hon. member for Villeneuve wanted to know who ordered the cleaning of them and the answer is that the cleaning of the rivers was authorized after inspection by a departmental official on April 28, 1959, and after an inspection was made by other officers. I trust that is the information required.
There are a few other matters I should like to refer to as we go along with the different items but at the moment I hope hon. members understand that it is a difficult thing to generalize on these specific questions.
In reply to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, and with this I will bring my remarks to a close, it is quite true that announcements are made. I have always felt that the important people in the government are the backbenchers. They form a very important part in the government. That applies also to hon. members on both sides; but the people of the Dominion of Canada by an overwhelming majority put the Tories in power in 1957. But that is not the point. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate makes an application to get something in his constituency, and other members do the same thing for their constituencies. It is not important to the local member who has done so much to get, say, a post office, a wharf,

a dock, a protection wall or a federal building-whatever it is-to get some credit for what he has done?
Therefore, being a person without ambition, I am not trying to make myself known across Canada and have the honour of making these announcements as Minister of Public Works. I have made a practice, and I do not think it is a new practice, that if a member wants to make an announcement of any local project he can do so. Of course if it is a national project or something which affects the national picture it should be made in the name of the Minister of Public Works; if it is a provincial matter it should be made in the name of the local minister on behalf of the Minister of Public Works, but if it is in a constituency, then by all means the member should make it and say something like "Mr. Joe Blow, on behalf of the Minister of Public Works, has pleasure in announcing that a post office will be built in"-wherever it is.
If hon. members of the opposition want to get in on this I would like to hear from them individually. In fact, the hon. member for Port Arthur asked me about it the other day and I said I would be delighted. He said, "How would it read?", and we arrived in fun at the conclusion that the effect of reading it might mean something like this: "Mr. Douglas Fisher, C.C.F. MP for Port Arthur, on behalf of the Conservative Minister of Public Works, the Hon. David Walker, has pleasure in announcing that the Conservative government at Ottawa is going to build a post office in this C.C.F. constituency". And that is the last I have heard from the hon. member for Port Arthur. He did not think that was a very good idea.
As I say, if there are any hon. members of the opposition who feel it would be a good idea, and perhaps the hon. member who made the suggestion does, perhaps they will let me know and on the next announcement we make in their riding, if they wish to try it out and find its effect, we will be happy to co-operate with the usual notice. There is nothing sinister about this; it is a nice friendly way of giving a person a chance.
Oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member for Ottawa West might like to do it too. We often have buildings constructed in his riding and I would be happy to give him the opportunity, as the well known Liberal member for that riding for all these years, of making an announcement on behalf of the Conservative government about what the Conservative government is doing in the Liberal riding of the hon. member.
Supply-Public Works
It does not do anything.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am afraid we on this side are not very much impressed by the confused and laboured explanation of the minister of his practice of including only Conservative members with himself in announcements of the type he has just mentioned. He has made it quite clear that if anybody else wishes to be included in this practice conditions will be laid down which would make it impossible for them to be associated with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Same conditions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It would be much more honest of the minister if he had merely said that he had decided to limit this kind of announcement to his own friends in the Conservative party, because that is obviously the effect of his remarks. That was made quite clear when he was good enough to tell the committee the form of the announcement which he proposed to the hon. member for Port Arthur. Obviously it was a form designed to make it quite impossible for the hon. member to accept, as the minister indicated. So that will do for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Has the Leader of the Opposition lost his sense of humour?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, it is because I have a sense of humour that I am able to appreciate the laboured efforts of the minister at being funny, because obviously he finds it funny. I also have enough of a sense of humour to appreciate the awakening awareness of the minister to the dangers and difficulties and misunderstandings, even the occasional unfairness, that one can get from headlines in the press. He will perhaps pardon me if I say that he did not show the same sensitiveness in earlier years when he, as a member of a committee of this house, was on the contributing rather than on the receiving end of headlines. However, I am glad to see his experience with ministerial responsibility is teaching him that headlines can perhaps even without intention at times be very unfair.
I rise to deal with just one point the minister raised because it concerns something I mentioned earlier in relation to my own constituency. In dealing with this matter the minister indicated his sympathy for and understanding of the problems of this particular area of Elliot Lake, for which he said the government were in no way responsible. We will have a chance to debate that when the trade and commerce estimates are up for consideration, so I will not dwell on that misstatement of fact at this time.

Supply-Public Works
He also said that the dock I mentioned at Cutler had been refused by the late government. It is perfectly clear, as I tried to show when I spoke a short time ago, that the arrangements which the previous government had been trying to make which would have made possible the building of this dock were of a manner which would not have placed the whole cost of the dock on the taxpayers but would have included in the expenditure for building the dock the mining industry and the coal importing company which would have used the dock. It is true that the arrangements were not concluded when the election took place in 1957. But it is also perfectly clear to anyone with any sense of reality at all that the possibility of concluding arrangements of that kind involving expenditures on the part of private industry were bound to fail when it became known to the uranium industry and the coal importing company that the leader of the Conservative party at that time who in a few months was to become Prime Minister of the country had promised during the campaign that the government would build that dock. I am asking the minister now why that particular promise, which was an unqualified one, has not been carried out, especially in the light of the new circumstances in the area.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I would be happy to answer that. The hon. Mr. Winters turned down the dock months before the general election in 1957.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have a letter on my file from the president of the coal company in 1958 giving me some information about the negotiations, and saying that at that date they could see no hope for the conclusion of these negotiations which had been continued on a different basis from that which Mr. Winters put forward.
In any event, the Prime Minister made the promise that when he became the head of the government that dock would be built. I mentioned that twice in the House of Commons. I made a specific statement that the Prime Minister had given his promise in 1957 and 1958 and no one on the other side of the house quarrelled with my statement of the Prime Minister's assurance. If the hon. gentleman would like to look at page 1415 of Hansard of November 22, 1957, when we were discussing the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys he can read my specific statement in which I attributed this promise to the present Prime Minister, and no comment was made denying that promise at the time. I repeated the assurance on July 4, 1958, as may be found on page 1916 on the estimates of the Minister of Public Works, and the minister of public

works of that day did not quarrel with my statement that the promise had been made.
I was looking at my press clippings and it is quite true that on May 12, 1957 the Prime Minister did, at a meeting in Espanola, Ontario make that statement. I also consulted my list of the promises made during that campaign and the subsequent one, and this particular promise was No. 113(b). Promise 113(a) was made at the same meeting in Espanola when the Prime Minister made another promise concerning this area. If the minister would like to look at the Ottawa Citizen for May 13, the Toronto Telegram for May 13 or the London Free Press for May 13, he would find a record of the meeting at Espanola at which the Prime Minister strongly criticized the government of the day for not building a dock at Cutler. He said at that meeting that if he was the head of the government he would ensure that Cutler became a port at which deep draught ships could call, because a dock would be built.
I ask the minister if that assurance is going to be carried out at the present time in view of the distressing situation which confronts Elliot Lake at the present time. The minister has said that the matter is under consideration, and I hope he will give it serious and sympathetic consideration. He has pointed out some of the difficulties, and I am not unsympathetic with regard to these difficulties. The chairman of the board of trustees of Elliot Lake was down here the other day, and I have reported to the minister what he said when he got back, namely that he had been informed that there was definite hope that the government's proposal for a dock for Cutler will be carried out. I hope this hope will be realized.
I have just been informed that the date of the Prime Minister speaking at Espanola when he made this interesting speech was May 11, not May 12, 1957. I apologize for this serious inaccuracy.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the date of the report of the meeting in the press, and whether the Leader of the Opposition can give us a quotation from one of those press reports?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, I can do that. I have a report from our own representative at the meeting-a very detailed report-but perhaps that would not impress the minister very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It will not. I can tell the hon. gentleman that right now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the minister will look al the Toronto Telegram of May 13-I have not the Telegram here, but I have sent for it- he will find a report which indicated they

were going to make Cutler a port, and as there was no dock or harbour there, that was interpreted by the community as a promise to build a dock. That interpretation was confirmed by the reports which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen and the London Free Press of May 13, 1957. The Canadian Press report of the meeting under the dateline Sault Ste. Marie says:
In both speeches he dwelt on local topics-the need for a dock at Cutler-
And in the London Free Press of May 13 the report said:
He (Mr. Diefenbaker) criticized the government for not building a dock at Cutler, on lake Huron, as a port for the uranium mining district.
Ther is no doubt in anyone's mind as to what the Prime Minister said, that there should be a dock at Cutler.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition would now like to modify his earlier statement this afternoon that the Prime Minister specifically promised that a dock would be built at Cutler.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, I do not modify my words. When the Prime Minister states that a community is going to be made into a port and when that community has no possible harbour, let alone a dock, and when the Prime Minister criticizes the government of the day for not building a dock, is that not a promise to build a dock?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wonder if the minister intends to give consideration to the questions I asked him about the lock at Carillon. His only reply earlier was that this was a matter for the Department of Transport but I cannot accept that because the application is made to the Department of Public Works under the Navigable Waters Act, part 1, which is the responsibility of the Minister of Public Works, and surely when the plans were approved over a year ago there was provision for the lock and the size of the lock as well as the depth to which the reaches on both sides of the lock were to be deepened.
I intend to be brief. In the course of my remarks I used an expression-a somewhat slang expression-when I said I thought I smelled a rat in connection with this whole matter, and now I believe I hold the proof in my hand, because the Minister of Transport indicated that it was not the lock at Carillon which was the important matter but the building of the new bridge which was announced by the former Quebec government. The newspaper La Presse of today, Wednesday, July 20, carries the headline: "Because there are no plans, construction of the bridges
Supply-Public Works between Montreal and lie Perrot will cease immediately." And the new minister of public works in Quebec had this to say-I will translate as well as I can as I go along- "Before asking for tenders it will be necessary to have plans and specifications drawn up either by the personnel of the department or by experts from outside the department."

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: This is the minister from Quebec, is it?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. The report goes on: "This government feels that it would be reasonable to invite contractors to tender." He did not say how long that would take. That is what I have feared all along, that there were no plans and specifications ready concerning this new bridge. How, therefore, could it be indicated by inference that the whole matter depends on that?
I have put this on record to show that there are no plans whatsoever in connection with this new bridge, and if there is a desire on the part of the government to provide for 14-foot navigation on the Ottawa it will have to meet the Quebec authorities and it will have to offer to pay to the Quebec authorities the cost of raising this bridge to the clearance necessary for ships of this draught, if this is the case. What did the plans which were filed by the minister's department say in so far as navigation was concerned? The minister was good enough to table some plans which I asked for in a notice of motion. I looked at them but I could find nowhere the information which I request now.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I shall be very happy to answer the hon. member for Laurier. As he knows, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act the Department of Public Works has to approve, and we are required to approve, the plans and site of a seaway bridge at Ste Anne de Bellevue in Quebec over the navigation channel. Our department has also consented to the starting of construction of a hydroelectric power development at Carillon, Quebec on the Ottawa river.
The clearance under the Ste Anne de Bellevue bridge is about the same as or higher than the existing clearance under the railway bridges belonging to the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways, located downstream.
The railways do not plan to make modifications to their bridges, at least at the present time. Clearance under those bridges has been the governing elevation for the bridges upstream on the Ottawa river, including the interprovincial bridge at Hawkesbury, Ontario.
The next point I should like to make is that the locks to be built into the Carillon

Supply-Public Works dam were designed to permit navigation drawing nine feet. However, vessels drawing up to 14 feet will be accommodated without major expenses when the need arises.
Finally, the present arrangement of the locks and the bridges appears satisfactory at the present time for the traffic, and such traffic as we -have at the present time is the only traffic expected to be developed on the Ottawa river in the near future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I thank the minister for that information. That is the information I have been trying to get in the questions that I asked. Now it is quite clear in my mind what the position is. It is exactly as I expected it would be, namely that provision is being made for nine-foot navigation all through the area from Ottawa down to the Ste Anne's bridge. When the minister states that the clearance at the new bridge will be the same as that at the C.N.R. and C.P.R. bridges now in existence it is clear I am informed that 14-foot navigation cannot go under the present C.N.R. and C.P.R. bridges now existing between Vaudreuil-Dorion and lie Perrot and the island of Montreal.
Of course, I cannot contradict the minister in so far as the statement he has given with regard to the new bridge at the west end of the islands is concerned because the present minister of public works in the Quebec government says that no plans and specifications have been prepared. That would seem to contradict what the minister has said, but I suppose that even although the plans and specifications have not been prepared, discussions would indicate that the clearance should be the same as under the other two bridges. I do not want to be unfair to the minister, but I would presume that is what took place, and it would follow from that that the clearance is for nine-foot and not 14-foot navigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: My hon. friend appears to have overlooked one thing. He is not suggesting that we are responsible for the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railway bridges? In connection with what we are doing it is clear that vessels drawing up to 14 feet will be accommodated without major expenses when the need arises. It is very important to know that, and I suppose that answers the question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I have just one word? It is very important, but the point is that if the nine-foot draft is in the lock now, or if you put it in the lock, it will become far more expensive to provide for 14-foot navigation after the power and navigation works have been completed. That is the point I made this morning and that is the point I again bring to the attention of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, we socialists are always interested in beautiful buildings. I drew to the minister's attention certain criticisms that had been made of the design of public buildings. I gave one illustration in the press, but I have drawn the minister's attention to other sources and suggest that possibly competitions could be held among Canadian architects for the design of larger public buildings intended to be erected by the minister's department. Would the minister mind informing the committee what the present policy is and what his reaction is to this suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Kootenay West, the proposal for design competition is not a new one, but it is always novel when it is expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I thank him again for making the proposal. I have examined the possibilities and the comment is as follows:
1.	Owing to the methods of operation of public departments it would be very difficult to set up a competition so that the competitors would appreciate the methods of working of the occupying departments. Unless they appreciate this the design that they will offer will leave much to be required. I believe that any winning design in such a competition would require drastic revision to make it meet the needs of the occupying departments.
2.	In order to hold a competition it would be necessary first to have an official statement of the requirements of buildings to be designed, a complete explanation of the operation and general plans which would meet the requirements of the occupying departments. A board of judges would have to be set up. The competition would have to be published and a suitable time allowed for the submission of designs. The board of judges would then have to meet and review all of the plans, and the judges themselves would have to be well acquainted with the requirements of the occupying departments; otherwise they could not judge the competition fairly. After the competition had been judged and the winner declared, then the winner would have to start in and prepare the working plans and specifications. As I indicated previously, I am sure the plans would have to be changed drastically from the competition design owing to the lack of knowledge on the part of the competitor.
For instance, in our new Sir Charles Tupper building, out at Hog's Back, to get rid of that smell of fish from the Department of Fisheries that we used to have in the west block where they did experiments, we had to have a special design. For the different facilities which we have in the Department

of Public Works and which the Department of Fisheries have, every facet and every need are specially designed. The hon. member for Kootenay West himself appreciates how difficult these things are.
Will the minister permit a question? Does he not know that there is no smell from good fish which is being cooked; it is just a good aroma?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I enjoy it too, particularly when I am fishing and catching fish, but still, will not the hon. member from New Brunswick, the brother of the new premier of New Brunswick-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member for Gloucester, whom I know better than I know his riding, I thought was the brother of the new premier of New Brunswick. I agree with what he has said. If he had been in the west block where these experiments with fish went on-I do not know what they did -I am sure he would agree it was an awful smell. That has been removed in our new building.
Would the minister permit another question?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Certainly. I had hoped to be facetious; perhaps I was not.
I am not being facetious. I should like to know how much it has cost the taxpayers to save the minister from having to smell the smell of fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I do not think this new plan cost anything extra. It was just a common-sense design of which a good architect was required to have knowledge. I could make some other comments to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He can probably imagine what they would be but this is my day of good behaviour and I will refrain from saying anything further.
Go ahead. They might help me in my campaign.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: For the leadership? Item 3: The Department of Public Works has for some years now prepared plans for the projects it has to produce. For instance, we have a wonderful plan for the new agricultural building.
Have you a site for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
That is the point. We have not got one that is satisfactory to everybody. May I repeat that the Department of Public Works has for some years prepared the plans for the projects it has to produce and over the years has acquired a knowledge of the working habits and customs of the various
Supply-Public Works departments and can plan their buildings much more rapidly than could any private architect who would be meeting the problem for the first time.
Socialism.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
It has been found more
practical to follow this method and to have consultants work from these preliminary plans supplied by the department. Item 4: I consider it quite a practical possibility to hold competitions where buildings would be in a classification such as museums, national theatres, convention halls, art galleries, etc. This, of course, will have some place, I would think, when the national capital commission goes into operation on some of its projects.

I wish to thank the minister for his explanation. I do not underestimate the difficulties. I was not suggesting for a moment that other people should replace the competent architects in the department but I did think there was some merit in the suggestion with respect to competitions for suitable exterior designs to which the requirements of any department could be adjusted. I had that in mind more than the details of construction.

Mr. Chairman, I almost wept when I heard the minister speak of taking a position in public life and being criticized. What struck me was that he did not speak that way when he was the leading man in the public accounts committee and was talking about other people. On Monday he spoke about Mr. Cormier, who was not here to defend himself, and condemned him as not being competent although he is known all over the world for his competency.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I am not complaining about anything that is said here at any time. I can hold my own. I was just making a few comments and I think most hon. members appreciate what I said about headlines about which even the hon. member for Villeneuve was shocked. That is all. I am not complaining particularly about anything the hon. member for Hull had to say. I never have complained. I do my best to hold my own in debate in the house. I have no apology for anything I said in the public accounts committee. If my hon. friend wants to repeat anything that was said either to me or about me or anything I said about anyone else I would be very happy if he would do so. I have no regrets and no apologies for what was said about me or what I said about anyone else. The public accounts committee was a very profitable one that year and,

Supply-Public Works without going into the matter again, may I say that it brought forth a great deal of benefit to the country.
Very profitable to the member for Rosedale.

I prefer what the minister has just said to what he said at the beginning of his remarks. Now he is himself. I had expected the minister would give me what I asked for on Monday, the names of those who inquired about Mr. Langlois and who made reports about work executed by Mr. Langlois. I think it is only fair that those names should be given so that Mr. Langlois may have a chance to prove that what has been said is wrong. I ask the minister now if he is willing to give those names.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, a summary of the information required in connection with Mr. Langlois is as follows: Ste. Fla vie school, bad roofing, general construction very poor, work done by Mr. Arthur Langlois; Mont Joli, bank building, work covering vault over stairs and garage and general alterations, work done a couple of years ago all very poorly executed; tiles loose, roof leaks, extremely bad plumbing; window hinges nailed instead of screws being used. That was also done by Mr. Arthur Langlois. Then there is the Belisle garage, Mont Joli; workmanship very rough, very amateurish, finishing very poor, and the contractor took double the normal time to complete. Shall I go on? The next case is Mont Joli, residence of Mr. Dumais, wood finishing very poor, joints very poor, and the owner had to take two months' holidays to supervise the work in order that it could be completed. General report: No use for building that requires any finishing.

I do not know about all these ouildings but now that the names of tne Duildings have been given we will have a cfiance to look at them and see what can ne done. The minister referred to a bank building involving a vault and some otner construction and said that the work was very poorly done. I have a letter here from tne architect in charge of this work for the bank which is completely contrary to what tne minister has said. I will read the letter: (Translation):
This is to certify that Mr. Arthur Langlois, general contractor, of Mont Joli, was responsible in the year 1956 for carrying out an enlargement and improvement work on the Banque Canadienne Nationale building at Mont Joli, P.Q., under contract from the bank.
The work consisted of building a new vault and carrying out considerable improvements to the building, both outside and inside, at a cost of approximately $35,000. It was done in a satisfactory way.

(Text):
This is a vault.
(Translation):
.. . and major improvement work was satisfactorily carried out both inside and outside the building.
(Text):
I produce a telegram from the C.N.R. signed by Mr. B. Martin, division engineer, stating that the work was done very satisfactorily. I also have a letter from Mr. R. M. Wickwire, building engineer for the C.N.R., stating that the work was successfully completed in a workmanlike manner to the complete satisfaction of the railway. What I should like to know now is this, I understand that the minister is a lawyer but he has forgotten one of the main principles of British law, that a man is not to be accused of anything without being given an opportunity to defend himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We are not accusing him of anything.

Oh, yes, the minister accused him in a letter he wrote on May 17.
(Translation):
The inquiry revealed that, though your financial means were considered adequate, the over-all construction of your buildings, we were told, is of very low quality. It has been noted that the finish of your work was very poor.
(Text):
So he is accusing the man of doing poor work under different contracts. He is accused of that and he is not given a chance to defend himself and to prove that the accusations to which the minister has referred are not correct. I think it is a very poor way to handle things. Now that we have the names of the buildings, we will try to get the names of these informants. Then, I believe Mr. Langlois will be in a position to prove he is a very competent contractor, as was affirmed by the engineer for the Canadian National Railways and by the architect of La Banque Canadienne Nationale. I hope that Mr. Langlois will not have to suffer any further damages because of the poor way in which the minister has handled the matter.
(Translation):
Now, Mr. Chairman, I shall take a few minutes to deal with another matter which has been raised in several instances in the house and which is of direct interest to the Minister of Public Works. The member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) has dealt with it, and it is of great concern to all members who represent constituencies along the Ottawa river, on both sides.
Mr. Chairman, we want to prepare for the development of the Ottawa river waterway. As the member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) has pointed out, plans are now being

drawn for the locks at Carillon, and those plans provide for a depth of only nine feet. However, to meet the requests of those who favour a deeper waterway, adequate for 5,000 ton ships, the depth would have to be at least 18 feet.
Plans are also being drawn for the construction of a bridge between Hull and Ottawa.
I hope that the sketches that were submitted-I do not know if they are the ones that are to be submitted shortly when the provincial ministers of public works will meet to deal with this important matter-will take into account the required clearance of the bridge, so that if, in the future, the Ottawa river were deepened, all the proposed new bridges will not have to be rebuilt entirely.
I admit that it will be necessary to raise the old bridges, because they were built before the deepening of the Ottawa river was even mentioned. I suggest that in all future works carried out on the Ottawa river, the Department of Public Works take into account the fact that sooner or later-and I hope that it will be sooner than later-the Ottawa river will be navigable a least as far as Hull, and that this deepening could subsequently be extended up to the head of lake Timiskaming.
Account must also be taken of the many industries along the Ottawa river, and of the possibility that the river may be navigable up to lake Timiskaming. In that event, the minister must call for plans providing for improvements along the Ottawa. He must also develop plans allowing for those future projects. It is said that to govern is to foresee; well it would be a good thing if the present minister planned now for future expansion along the Ottawa river.
I also claim that, because the Ottawa river is navigable, several locations on it should be protected against erosion. Every year, the municipality of Gatineau Point is subject to flooding which reaches far inland. It has been the same at Templeton and at Angers where water eroded as much as 200 feet out of certain lands. Floods have also caused damage at Masson and elsewhere.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister to take those factors into account, and to give consideration to that area which is in great need of protection and improvement.
Supply-Public Works
(Text):

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should just like to clear up one point, Mr. Chairman. I gather I was not successful in convincing the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the Prime Minister had, in fact, made a specific promise regarding the dock at Cutler. I should like to try to do so by quoting from a press authority which will be unquestioned by hon. gentlemen opposite, the Toronto Telegram. The report in the Toronto Telegram is dated May 13, 1957, and is datelined "Parry Sound". It reads:
Unloading new pledges as he went along, Mr. Diefenbaker in the various centres he spoke committed a Conservative government after June 10 to several important actions.
Included in those was this one, which reads:
Parry Sound-Improvements would be made to the wharves and docks in Parry Sound and at Cutler to handle large shipping upon completion of the St. Lawrence seaway.
Since before this statement was made the only dock at Cutler was a very small one capable of handling only rowboats, and small craft, it is quite clear that this was a promise to construct a dock at Cutler which would handle large ships upon completion of the St. Lawrence seaway.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is that sentence in the article in quotation marks?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is a report in the Toronto Telegram in which the Toronto Telegram made this statement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I just ask one question? I think all of us believe the minister to be honest. Would he let me have my New York Central brochure back?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

I have another item which I should like at this time to bring to the attention of the Minister of Public Works. I feel that this is the time for the minister to give to the house all the information he has on this particular item. What I have in mind is a project which is of great interest to the entire population of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, namely the Chignecto canal. For the last three years the Minister of Transport has been referring in this house to a preliminary report or a preliminary engineering estimate on the Chignecto project which was being prepared by the Department of Public Works; and here I am using the Minister of Transport's own words.
6614	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works On March 4 of last year, about 16 months ago, the Minister of Transport advised the house that, arising out of the work that had been done to date by the Department of Public Works, he had asked that certain other estimates be worked out. It was only in April of this year that a report was issued, prepared for the Chignecto canal committee and resulting from a preliminary investigation into the economic aspect of such a project. We were informed in this House of Commons by the Prime Minister on April 13 of this year, as reported at page 3188 of Hansard, that following that report a formal request would be made for a full scale economic study by the federal government-and I insist on those word's "by the federal government"- in order to determine the economic feasibility of the Chignecto canal. On June 22 I was surprised to learn from the newspapers, as I happened to be away from Ottawa on that day, the following information. I read here a report from the Gleaner dated June 22, 1960. It is headed "Works Minister Tells Commons of Canal Plan" and it reads in part as follows:
Ottawa (CP)-The federal and New Brunswick governments will share the cost of a study of the feasibility of building the Chignecto canal, works minister Walker said today.
I ask the minister this question: Why should the province of New Brunswick be called upon to pay 50 per cent of the cost of an investigation or a study on a project which, according to the Minister of Transport, was under way for the last two and a half years to three years? Why should the province of New Brunswick be called upon-is it because there was an election to follow within the next five or six days?-to pay 50 per cent of the cost of this survey when over a year and a half ago the federal government undertook on its own to pay the full cost of the survey for the Prince Edward Island causeway? I think that we from New Brunswick have a right to an explanation from the minister as to the decision that was reached asking the province of New Brunswick to pay 50 per cent of the cost of the survey for a project which comes entirely under federal jurisdiction.
Before this first item is passed I hope the Minister of Public Works will give to the house a full report of the work which was supposed to have been done to date, the work which has been mentioned here in this chamber by the Minister of Transport, as being done by the Department of Public Works. We should have a report on this survey. If nothing was done, we have a right to find out why the Minister of Transport made such statements in the house. If the province of New Brunswick is to pay 50 per cent of the 

cost of such a survey, I again ask this question: Why did the Prime Minister on April 13 of this year make a statement in the House of Commons that, following the report of the Chignecto canal committee, a formal request will be made for a full scale economic study by the federal government-and I insist on those words "by the federal government"-[DOT] to determine the economic feasibility of the Chignecto canal?
We who are from New Brunswick know that the Chignecto canal is a "must" for the economy of our province. We know that statements have been made that following the construction of the canal our great industrialist in New Brunswick, namely Mr. K. C. Irving, is prepared to go ahead and develop industries to the extent of over $100 million. Mr. Chairman, I want to take advantage of this opportunity today, July 20, to pay my respects and homage to Mr. Irving who has today in Saint John the official opening of the new oil refinery. I received an invitation to attend this formal opening but I regret that, owing to the work of this House of Commons, I was unable to be there. However, I want to pay my homage to Mr. Irving who contributes so largely to the development of New Brunswick today, and particularly to the Saint John area.

I just want to say one thing in connection with the matter I raised concerning the city of Cornwall and the team which the two departments, namely the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works, have established with reference to port development along the whole St. Lawrence seaway area. I hope the minister did not misunderstand me earlier when I brought this matter to the attention of the committee. I have no objection-not the slightest-to any credit for what is being done now or will be done in the future being given to the hon. member for Stormont. But I would like the minister to remember that for 18 years I was a member of that community and I still have very close ties with it. He will pardon me if I say that for a period of 20 years my father was a member of the city council. He was its mayor and then he ran for parliament in 1921 and was defeated by less than 100 votes. He ran, I must say, as a Liberal candidate of course.
I do not want any credit for anything which will be done for this community. My only purpose in rising was that I think there is a very serious situation in Cornwall with reference to economic conditions,

and I am sure that notwithstanding what I have said concerning the team the minister will want to see to it, and his officers particularly, that that community is given every opportunity to rehabilitate itself. With so many questions put to him the minister did not have the opportunity to reply to the appeal which I made to him.
I ask him if, in the course of his reply before the first item goes through, he will not ask his officers to give particular consideration to the facilities which are required for this community, and if he will I can assure him I will be perfectly satisfied, having done what I believe it is my simple duty to do.
I would also like to add that there is information which a former minister of the crown has in his possession, either from memory or because of his experience, that fortunately or unfortunately others may not have. I tried to avail myself of that information when I brought the matter to his attention, and it was exclusively with that in mind.
The statement is made from time to time that I want to go back and run in the constituency of Stormont and that that is why I am particularly interested in it. There is no truth whatsoever to that statement. I am perfectly happy to be the member for the constituency of Montreal-Laurier. My law office is in Montreal; I have a residence there as well; and I would not want anyone in the constituency of Montreal-Laurier to think for one moment that I am not perfectly happy with my constituents. But I feel it my duty none the less because of my long association with the community that is-
That sounds like an annual meeting in your riding.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not an annual meeting in my own riding. I have indicated why I brought the matter up and I think the minister, by the way in which he has received the remarks which I have made, has taken them in the right vein. I know that under the circumstances he will realize I am rising because of my long association with it and for no other reason whatsoever. I am sure he will ask the team and his own officers to give this particular problem the attention which I think it deserves.

Mr. Chairman, when speaking for this group on the first day when the minister's estimates were before the committee, and because of this group's particular interest in satisfactory working conditions, I dealt very briefly with the question of air conditioning. Would the minister when he replies inform the house of the department's policy with respect to the installation of air 79951-0-417
