Mr. Chairman, I rise to make what seems to be an annual appeal for a particular dredging project near the city of Kingston. The place in question is not in the riding of the city of Kingston so obviously it is not for my riding that I appeal. The dredging project which I have mentioned before is one which the minister has heard of on many occasions, and it is located about 25 miles east of lake Ontario. In the planning of the seaway they apparently forgot to dredge a small half-mile section 25 miles east of Kingston, and by leaving this section undredged they have forced shipping on the St. Lawrence seaway to go through the United States channel.
We have recently had a bill before the house amending the Canada Shipping Act in order to regulate the pilotage in the great lakes basin, which is the area between St. Regis, opposite Cornwall, and the head of the lakes. In this section between St. Regis and Kingston, where once only about 20 miles of the waterway east of the area was in United States waters, today because we have located the locks on the United States side and have not dredged this one section to which I refer almost the entire section between St. Regis and lake Ontario is now through the United States channel. I think this is an important point. The dredging of this small section will require a very small amount of money and by so dredging we could bring the extreme western end of the St. Lawrence river back on the Canadian side.
I bring this to the attention of the minister because Kingston is a port from which we ship or bring in about one and three quarter million tons of cargo a year. The deep draught ships which come in and go out of Kingston harbour are now required to go into lake Ontario and down what is the United States channel. I ask the minister to take this small dredging project into consideration so that Canadian shipping can follow that channel to the St. Lawrence river which it has followed since shipping began, and bring it back on the Canadian side giving those opportunities for industry which these communities deserve.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to ask for something in particular for my own riding at this time although there is a need for dockage and dredging on the Welland ship canal which has been

Supply-Public Works brought about by the seaway. However, there are negotiations underway at the present time and I think they are going along quite successfully, so I will not mention that further at this time.
However, I would like to draw to the attention of the minister a problem which has been brought to my attention in connection with the parliament buildings. There appears to be a great lack of restroom facilities and lavatories for tourists and visitors who come to the building. I understand there is no particular place for that purpose, and I suggest to the minister that when the west block is remodelled facilities of this kind might be provided there.
I recall that some two years ago I made a suggestion about replacing the steps in front of the building. That has been done, and it is a very fine job. I would just like to refer the suggestion 1 have made to the minister for his consideration.

Can I ask the Minister of Public Works whether the allocation of space in the centre block as far as the security police are concerned comes under his jurisdiction or whether it comes under that of the Speaker?

speechtext: The Speaker.

I think when the minister answered the remarks made by various members who have had occasion to say something on this first item he failed to answer one important question which was put to him when I made my remarks on Monday evening. I asked him if he could justify the fact that there was such an important decrease in the work done by the department at a time when unemployment is reaching alarming proportions and the outlook is none too promising. I think this is one of the most important questions which has been asked during the debate; the minister should have taken note of that question and justified, if he could, the position of the government with regard to it.
There is a further question I wish to raise. In one of the answers the minister gave this afternoon he said that when I was saying that the causeway between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick would not be built in the near future I was only joking. I was not joking at all. As a matter of fact I have read very carefully the report which was given by the deputy minister of public works in the speech he delivered in Prince Edward Island.
In this report it was stated that well known firms, besides many departments of government, had studied very thoroughly the effect that such a construction would have on the

high and low water levels of the strait, the damage that might result to private properties and harbours, and so on. A study had also been made of the surrounding land, and of the movement of the ice, and of which site would be most appropriate for the construction. Soundings and borings had been made, together with analysis of the stone in various neighbouring quarries. In addition designs had been prepared for various types of construction.
I am asking the minister what further technical information he needs in order to be able to make an approximate estimate of the cost of this project and to say whether or not it is economically feasible. In the past two years we have spent more than $600,000 on this scheme. I hope the minister will listen to me, because I was not joking when I spoke. After all, I am an engineer. I know a little about construction, although I am not an expert. I was not joking at all when I mentioned what I did.
I think the department or the government is trying to bury this project. I think that in the circumstances the minister himself should have taken the responsibility of going to Prince Edward Island and explaining the whole situation to the population. The minister will recall that a question was asked in the house by the hon. member for North-umberland-Miramichi. Part of the question was this:
Was the sole purpose of his visit to deliver a speech.
The answer given by the Minister of Public Works was, no. I can understand why the answer was in the negative. I think the purpose of sending the deputy minister down there was to bury their project. There was another question, part 5, which asks:
Were there any other passengers in the aircraft and, if so, who were they?
I think the names that appeared in the answer were the names of the honorary pallbearers of this project-the Minister of Fisheries and the three hon. members from Prince Edward Island plus a member of the press gallery, an official of the Department of Fisheries and another from the Department of Transport.
I repeat that I have read the report made by the deputy minister to the people of Prince Edward Island and I cannot see why at this stage after we have spent more than $600,000
__and we are being asked to spend another
$50,000-it should not be possible for the consulting engineers in co-operation with the departments of government concerned to establish an approximate price for this project. Unless the minister can tell me there is some important technical information

which is still lacking I think the minister owes some further explanation to the committee.
I have a further comment to make, and it has to do with the question which was asked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate on January 21, 1960. The question was as follows:

I wonder if I could ask the Minister of Public Works whether in view of the statement he is reported to have made, which appears in Tuesday's Halifax Chronicle-Herald, that an estimate of $90 million for the Prince Edward Island causeway was too low, and now obsolete, and that an estimate of $450 million was too high and fantastic, he would now tell the house what cost surveys to date have revealed as to the probable estimated cost of the project.
I would ask the minister to note his words "too high and fantastic". In his answer, the hon. gentleman suggested that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate should put his question on the order paper and my hon. friend replied that he would be glad to do so.
The next day, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate came back with another question:
Then I ask the minister how he was able to say that figures which have been published were fantastic?
Then, the Minister of Public Works answered:
If the hon. member wants an answer to that question I do not mind at all giving it. The original estimate as to the cost of this causeway was $60 million without railway accommodation, or $90 million with such accommodation. That was some time ago. Since then our research and investigation into this project has got under way and we have met with tremendous problems, which of course would greatly increase the cost of such a causeway. Consequently, until these problems are analysed and the final reports made it would be impossible for me to come up with another estimate. Nevertheless I do say that the figure which has been bruited about-that it will be between $480 million and $540 million-is to my mind and to the minds of the engineers of my department a fantastic estimate. It is much too high.
The minister will recall that he said the $90 million was much too low; the $480 million was fantastic. Now, he must have had in mind some kind of a figure at which he arrived in consultation with the engineers on the technical information that they have received. That is the reason why, after reading this report and reading all through the answers that he gave to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I say we have now, after two years' study-and if I remember correctly the study of the causeway was started at least two years ago; it was started in 1956-and after spending $500,000 or $600,000, we are entitled to know, even if the estimated cost at this time, with the 79951-0-417*
Supply-Public Works technical information we have, is about $10 million, $15 million or $20 million apart, what is the estimated cost of the project, either the causeway, a combination of a bridge and causeway or a bridge, because I understand the idea of a tunnel was dropped, according to the speech delivered by the deputy minister of public works.
Again I ask the minister in all sincerity to tell the committee whether he has not at this time all the technical information required to give us a real approximate cost of the project. If not, I want to know from him what are the technical details which are missing which are required by the consulting engineers and the engineers of the three departments concerned with the study of the project. I ask the minister once again to give us this information and not brush me aside. I tell him that I have been checking on this project, because I spent some time in studying the report. I am quite sure that at this time we have all-and I repeat it-the technical information necessary to arrive at a fair estimate of the cost of the project.
There is the question of the strength of the ice in the strait. I know this is being studied at the moment, but I do not think it would affect very seriously the cost of the project. I think research is being carried on into this matter at the moment. I think the minister's engineers will have these data either from Canada or the United States. Will the minister give us this information?

What I have to raise at this moment is most picayune in comparison with that raised by the previous hon. member. If the minister is going to answer all questions at once I should like to draw a matter to his attention. I understand he is in charge of the centre block which houses the House of Commons and the Senate. It is my understanding that this building comes under the Department of Public Works. Although this matter is picayune, I want to raise it because it is the only chance I shall have. In what I have to say I have no reference whatsoever to any member of this house or any party in the house.
What I suggest to the minister is that he bring in somebody to do something about the advance of earwigs and cockroaches in this building. I raised this matter some five years ago, if I remember correctly, and about two days later a fumigation took place. That is the reason I said I am not referring either to members or to parties; but I do suggest to the Minister of Public Works, under whom this building comes, that there is need for fumigation of certain areas of the centre

Supply-Public Works block because of the encroachment of earwigs and cockroaches. Conditions have reached such a state that if fumigation does not take place fairly soon you will not need a fumigator, you will need a big game hunter. I draw this to the minister's attention, and if I cannot tell him I know certain members can tell him where to search.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon the minister gave some names and some information about work done by Mr. Langlois. Can he tell me where he got this information, and who did the research for the information because I have established that so far as one instance is concerned it is completely untrue since the architect of the bank said that the work was very satisfactory. So far as the others are concerned, I do not know but I should like to know who did the research.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to impose myself again on the committee. I have been up twice already thinking I was imposing for the last time. Is there any other hon. member who wishes to speak before I do because if there is I will sit down?
I am going to answer the questions of all hon. members. The hon. member for Gloucester asked about the Chignecto canal. All I know is that I negotiated with the former premier of New Brunswick, and so did our Prime Minister. He was a great advocate of the canal and he wanted an economic feasibility study made. Of course, as the hon. member for Gloucester knows, there have been a great many studies, but the former premier pressed the matter and we finally arranged to have an economic feasibility survey performed. We did not expect the cost to be too great, and the province and the dominion would pay 50 per cent of the cost.
In connection with this, the hon. member for Gloucester will be glad to know that we are receiving the co-operation of the Department of Public Works and of the Department of Transport and the P.F.R.A., particularly the maritime marshland rehabilitation branch. They are down there all the time and are very helpful. Then the mines and technical surveys department is also interested. We have already had the first meeting and unless the new government under the aegis of the namesake of the hon. member for Gloucester reneges we are going to go ahead with the survey.

Before the minister leaves this question, how can he reconcile the statement which he has just made that an agreement has been made with the province of New Brunswick for the province to pay 50 per cent of the cost of the survey with the statement made in this house on April 13

by the Prime Minister when he said, and I quote his words as reported at page 3188 of Hansard:
-following that report-
The report of the Chignecto canal committee.
-a formal request will he made along the lines indicated-
In other words, a formal request for a full scale economic study by the federal government to determine the economic feasibility of the Chignecto canal. The Prime Minister stated in the house in answer to questions put to him that the survey would be made by the federal government and that it would be an economic survey to study the feasibility of the Chignecto canal. How can the minister reconcile his statement that the province of New Brunswick will be called upon to pay 50 per cent of the cost? Prince Edward Island was not called upon to pay 50 per cent of the cost of the causeway survey. This is a federal project. If it were a joint undertaking on the part of the province and the federal government I would say it would be perfectly all right to have New Brunswick pay 50 per cent of the cost, but this is a federal project.
Ontario and Quebec were not called upon to pay 50 per cent of the cost of the St. Lawrence seaway so why should New Brunswick be called upon to pay 50 per cent of the cost of what is entirely a federal project which should be paid for entirely by the federal government? That is the explanation I should like to get from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
That was the agreement
reached. I am glad to note the hon. member's remarks on the subject but I would have preferred to have his remarks in advance of the solution or even after it was announced in the house. When I made the announcement I think it was made very clear that it was to be a federal survey with respect to which the province and the dominion were each to pay 50 per cent.
And it was suggested by us at the time, as the minister will recall, that the federal government should pay it all.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I do not remember that.
If the minister will look it up he will see that I asked a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Did my hon. friend make that suggestion?
I did because the hon. member for Gloucester was elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The province of New Brunswick volunteered to pay 50 per cent. Of course, the present government may have reneged.
We are finally getting an eruption from the volcano.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It is still a federal project. But for years the federal government-I am not being political-has been importuned to have a feasibility study made and, without naming names, no government has been willing to do so. The premier of New Brunswick was very anxious that this should be done and in order to induce the federal government to do so offered to pay 50 per cent. For the first time that I know of a real feasibility study is being undertaken.

Would the minister permit a question? Was the minister's attention ever drawn to the Canadian Press story of the Prime Minister's statement at Saint John, New Brunswick, on May 3, 1957? The report I happen to have in front of me is from the Ottawa Journal of May 4, but at that time the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
On maritime area issues, he said a Conservative government at Ottawa would give the provinces a better tax-sharing deal and carry out a complete investigation into the feasibility of the decades old proposal for a Chignecto canal to link the bay of Fundy with Northumberland strait. The survey would determine "whether the dream of past generations can become the reality of the future" in the Chignecto isthmus linking New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
That was the Prime Minister's statement, a complete investigation into the feasibility of the proposal. That is what the right hon. gentleman promised when he was giving assurances to get into office, and we will recall that it was only last week that the right hon. gentleman boasted in the house that his assurances were always kept. Why did he not keep this one? Why did the government not keep it? Why are they making a relatively poor province like New Brunswick pay half the cost because, as the minister said, the former premier of that province importuned the federal government to carry out something the Prime Minister promised the people of New Brunswick before he became Prime Minister?
And it is a federal project too.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I do not profess, of course, to answer for the Prime Minister, but I think the government of Canada has made very generous financial arrangements for the province of New Brunswick as well as the provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. We are carrying out
Supply-Public Works an economic feasibility study and the fact that the province is paying 50 per cent of the cost does not derogate in any way from the fact that an economic feasibility study is being carried out in accordance with the promise the Prime Minister made. In any event, he did not tell them in that statement that he would do it free of charge to the province.
The hon. member for Laurier has made a very telling request on behalf of Cornwall, and in giving credit to the present member for Stormont I am not in any way derogating from the good will and sincerity of the hon. member for Laurier. As a matter of fact, I can assure him that the department has already been instructed to give the question of Cornwall prior consideration and high priority on consideration. The remarks of the hon. member for Laurier have certainly assisted very greatly in the representations which have already been made to us by the present hon. member for Stormont. I can assure him that nothing he has said has fallen on deaf ears.
In reply to the hon. member for Kootenay West all new buildings have the ducts inserted in them for air conditioning but at the present time we are using the next best thing to air conditioning which is forced ventilation so that constantly moving fresh air is going through the buildings. As the hon. member for Kootenay West must know, the actual insertion of air conditioning is a tremendous expense. I have been amazed at the expense involved, and on the advice of my deputy I have personally taken the responsibility of turning down air conditioning because we feel that at this particular stage the expenditure is not warranted. If we are flush some day and great prosperity returns and we have no problems of balancing the budget, we have the ducts available for inserting air conditioning. In some centres where the condition is really serious such as one building in Windsor, we have installed air conditioning.
I can tell the hon. member for Kingston that Wolf island channel dredging is a matter to which we are giving special consideration. He has been to my office with delegations from the Kingston area, and the matter is being very seriously considered. I will save my reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East to the end.
Do I understand that the minister is not going to answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I will answer but I wish to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Levis first. The hon. member for Levis asked me why we cut $25 million from last year's public works budget. There are two reasons.

Supply-Public Works The first reason is, of course, that in the two previous years, in an effort to get out of the recession, a great spending program, although a proper and well directed spending program, was initiated. It was felt that this could not be kept up forever and that it was a very good thing to cut back this year because we had hopes of having a very prosperous year and, aside from the unemployment figures, the gross national product is going to be exceptionally good.
As my hon. friend also knows, when the Minister of Finance made his budget address the hon. member for Levis was one of those who voted for a balanced budget. I am not always in favour of the suggestions made by the Minister of Finance. Sometimes we are at odds. Naturally, all the backbenchers on my side of the house and the other side who want things I am convinced they should have. Sometimes I have to bow to the Minister of Finance and you are quite right when you suggest that.
The minister is forgetting the promises that were made in 1957 and 1958.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Hon. members not only got promises, but they got results. The benefits of a balanced budget are obvious, even to my engineering friend the hon. member for Levis. I do not need to go into that. What would have happened in the country so far as finance is concerned? We have to have our financial institutions operating properly if we want to have business operating as well as possible. I need not go into that. It has been very beneficial. I do not know that anybody has suffered particularly at the hands of the Department of Public Works.
In so far as the causeway is concerned, I cannot say anything more than I have said. If my hon. friend suspects that the object of this tremendous study that has been conducted is for the purpose of burying it, I must say then that he is indulging in the kind of thinking in which the Liberal government indulged for 22 years when they did nothing about the causeway. He will agree with that. The hon. member should try to get the new look, the new view. We must wait for the national research council to make its report, and when it does we will be in a position to come to this committee with the report. The last thing we want to do is to bury this project.

I should like to ask the minister what the technical information is that the department needs in order to make an estimate and ascertain whether this project would be economical. That is all I am asking. I gave my reasons for asking this question.

The minister said $90 million is too low and $480 million is too high. Now he must have relied on some information in order to make that statement. I believe this information could be obtained from the reports the deputy minister made when he went to Prince Edward Island. I think we have all the information we need to state whether this project is economical.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: There is a difference of opinion between my hon. friend, who is a distinguished engineer-
I am not a distinguished engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: -and the engineers of my department. Then, if you are not, perhaps you will concede that these other engineers might be.
Once again I am just asking the minister what the technical information is that is required. Is it the ice loading on piers?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I have already told my friend that the national research council has many studies under consideration. First, and most important is the effect of the tremendous currents which flow through that area of the causeway; what the effect would be of the ice floes on the causeway, the effect on the adjacent lands and how much of the adjacent shore is going to be destroyed; how it is going to be built up; how the fish are going to be affected by the change. All these things are under consideration.
As the result of the report from the national research council-
It is in the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: -we will decide how we are going to plan the structure of this causeway. Until that is done, however, I would only be guessing if I were to make an estimate.

The report contains an estimate of the damages that are going to be caused by the causeway. They have been estimated at $13 million. I have read the report. I wonder if the minister has read it? I am not joking; it is in there.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I know my friend is not joking; he has told me that many times. He will have to excuse me if I sometimes think he is.
I have been in this house for 20 years and I know what it is to brush somebody aside.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I would never, under any circumstances, brush my friend aside. May I say this? Somebody estimated the cost at $90 million and somebody estimated it at

$400 million. I said one is too little and the other is too great. That is the best I can do.
How can the minister say that before having this technical information? He cannot.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: My friend asked me now to estimate it, and then in the next breath he tells me I cannot estimate it. What does he mean? I want to please him but I do not want to be nonsensical.
I did not say that. I said, how can the minister say that $90 million is too low and $480 million is too high? There must be a figure in between those two figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: There is.

I am asking the minister on what he is basing his statement when he says that one figure is too low and one figure is too high? He must have some information, otherwise he is speaking without foundation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
We have a lot of information. We have sufficient information from our engineers to say that $90 million is too low and $400 million is too high. However, we have not all the information necessary to be able to prognosticate how much the causeway will cost. My friend would be the first to tell me that I am not an engineer, and I must be a lawyer if I would make a guess like that because only a lawyer would have the temerity to do that. No engineer would ever do so.
Then the hon. member for Vancouver East asked me about certain things in the house. I took it that he was speaking not about human beings but about some other animal life. In reply, I should like to say that this matter is within the purview of the Sergeant-at-Arms. I am sure he would be glad to go into the matter. He has heard the discussion which took place tonight. We have charge of the elevator service and we are also in charge of certain repair work. Of course, the Sergeant-at-Arms, on behalf of the Speaker of this house, may request us to do repairs or make alterations. The House of Commons, and particularly the centre block, is within the particular purview of the Speaker and the Sergeant-at-Arms. I shall certainly bring this matter to the attention of both parties.

At the same time I would ask the minister to take note of something which irritates many members who, perhaps, do not speak about it. There is one elevator, very important to the members of the house-I refer to the one on our right, here-and it goes out of operation at the most important hour of the day in so far as hon. members
Supply-Public Works are concerned. Perhaps the minister would consider the replacement of that elevator which is very important to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is within our province, and we will certainly do that.

I appreciate that the minister has given the house part of the information which I requested concerning the Chig-necto canal. The Minister of Transport, I repeat, has been making statement after statement for the last two and a half years that an engineering survey was being conducted by the Department of Public Works in order to determine the feasibility of the Chignecto canal. I should like the minister to tell this house what work has been carried on by his department. What was the cost of the work? How many men or how many engineers were employed on this survey? According to statements by the Minister of Transport, this survey was being conducted by officials of the Department of Public Works.
If this survey is partly completed, why should the province of New Brunswick be called upon to pay 50 per cent of the cost for the completion of such a survey? If there was no survey, if nothing has been done by the officials of the Department of Public Works, then let the minister tell us that so we will know where we stand. I think we have a right to know. How far has this survey been carried out, and what has been done? How many officials or employees have taken part in this survey?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In reply to the hon. member, may I ask if he would like us to call off the economic feasibility project or survey? We would be glad to do so without charge. Is that what you have in mind?
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, may I say this? I think this is a good way for the minister to use his usual practice to brush off questions which are being asked of him.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No.

If the minister wants to call it off, all right. I did not make any suggestion that the survey should be called off. In fact, my suggestion was the very opposite. I asked the minister to advise the house what work has been done so far. I have asked the minister this question. If the survey has been initiated by the federal government, according to statements which were made in reply to questions which were asked of the Minister of Transport, why should the province be called upon to pay 50 per cent of the cost for that survey?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that anything that has been done prior to

Supply-Public Works the agreement with the premier of New Brunswick will not be charged to anybody. I can assure him of that. But he can appreciate that we are going to use all available material from every source in making the survey. That is one of the reasons why it should not be too expensive. We are going to give ourselves the benefit of all the information from every department which I have named to the hon. member. As to what has been done to date by the new committee, as I say, the matter is just in its organizational stage.

That is not what the hon. member for Gloucester asked at all. The Minister of Transport told us in 1958 that at that time in 1958-and I will try to put this slowly so that the minister can take it in-that the Department of Public Works was already then engaged in an engineering study. What the hon. member for Gloucester asked was how many persons were engaged in that study, how much it had cost up to date. That is precise, concrete information. That is an accounting of the expenditure of the taxpayers' money for the obtaining of which the committee of supply exists. That is what we want an answer to.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I will not tell my hon. friend that he has misunderstood what was said because I do not know what was said. I was not the minister at the time. But I can assure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that to date the Department of Public Works has not been engaged in any economic study, that is to say in recent years. I do not know what happened before the hon. member's government took power 22 years ago. I do not know what happened then. But we certainly have not been engaged in any economic feasibility study of the Chignecto canal. Perhaps my hon. friend' has some quotations from Hansard that he could refer me to.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It was not by me.

I refer to page 1593 of Hansard of March 4, 1959. The Minister of Transport advised this house that, arising out of the work that had been done to date, he had asked for certain other estimates to be worked out by the Department of Public Works. I want to repeat what I said once again, namely that the Minister of Transport has led the House of Commons to believe this for the last two and a half years. In reply to questions which were addressed to him by members of the opposition, including my colleague the hon. member for Northumber-land-Miramichi and myself, he told the house that a survey was actually being carried out.


I have not that reference in Hansard in front of me but on three or four occasions we were told that an economic survey to determine the feasibility of the Chignecto canal was being carried out by the Department of Public Works and in good faith we accepted that statement from the Minister of Transport. Tonight we find from the Minister of Public Works that to his knowledge no officials of his department at any time were employed in such a survey. This is a clear example of what we of the opposition have to face from the present government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Will my hon. friend be good enough to read that clause again? I would ask him just to read it again.
A study, not a survey.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It is a short sentence.

On March 4, as found at page 1593 of Hansard-I have not Hansard in front of me at the moment-the Minister of Transport advised the house that, arising out of the work that had been done to date, he had asked that certain other estimates be worked out-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Just a minute.
-by the Department of Public Works.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Just a minute. Do you mind my interrupting? The words are "arising out of the work that has been done to date". He does not say that was done by the Department of Public Works.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No; he does not. Would my hon. friend carry on from there? After the phrase "arising out of the work that has been done to date", will my hon. friend read on from there?

I want to state again that the Minister of Transport has in this House of Commons been referring to a preliminary engineering estimate on the Chignecto project which was being prepared by the Department of Public Works. This can be found-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, may I say this? I know that my hon. friend does not want to mislead the committee. He has read one clause "arising out of the work that has been done to date". I ask him whether he will be good enough, for the benefit of the members of his party as well as of ours, to read the next clause. We want to have fairness here and we want to be fair to hon. members opposite. So far there is no indication in what he has read that the Department of Public Works did the work. Would the hon. member now read on?
Mr. Chairman,-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Will you read on?
-I repeat-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Will the hon. member hand it to me and I will read it?
I have not Hansard in front of me at the moment but I will get it. I will produce tomorrow the whole of the quotation of the statements made by the Minister of Transport.
Shame.
There is no shame there. You will find that the records are there to prove it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
While we are getting the Hansard reference in connection with the statement of the Minister of Transport about which the Minister of Public Works seems to be skeptical, perhaps he will be more impressed if I put on the record a statement made by the Prime Minister when he said, according to a Canadian Press report of a meeting on May 3, 1957 at Saint John:
On maritime area issues, he-
That is the Prime Minister.
-said a Conservative government at Ottawa would ... carry out a complete investigation into the feasibility of the decades old proposal for a Chignecto canal to link the bay of Fundy with Northumberland strait.
The survey would determine "whether the dream of past generations can become the reality of the future"-
The minister now tells us that his department has done nothing since that time in connection with that survey.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
My friend the hon. member for Gloucester will be glad to learn that I have here Hansard of March 4, 1959. As indicated at page 1593, Mr. McWilliam asked question No. 35 which was as follows:
1.	Has a survey been made on the feasibility of the construction of the Chignecto canal?
2.	If so, has enough data been compiled to determine the feasibility of this project?
3.	If not, when is it expected the data will be completed?
The answer given was as follows. I ask my hon. friend to note this answer. It is all here:

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might deal with all three parts of this question in one answer. The hon. member is, I know, aware that over the years there have been many studies made of this proposal, the earliest one reported being dated 1822. Because of this I rather think the inquiry arises from the statement I made in the house on August 28 last when the estimates of the Department of Transport were under consideration. At that time I said the Department of Public Works had been asked to give us a preliminary engineering estimate on the cost of the Chignecto project, on the basis of which 79951-0-418
Supply-Public Works
it was proposed to have another economic study made and that I would report the findings to my colleagues.
Arising out of the work that has been done to date, I have asked that certain other estimates be worked out, and it is consequently not possible to say at present when a complete report will be put before me.
There is nothing there to say that.

That is the most absurd thing, Mr. Chairman. In August of 1958 the Minister of Transport told us that he had asked the Department of Public Works to make this study. That is what appears there, on August 28, 1958. He told us in the committee that he had asked the Department of Public Works. Then he says in the next paragraph:
Arising out of the work that has been done to date-
This statement was made the following March.
Arising out of the work that has been done to date.
If the word of the Minister of Transport means anything which the minister seems to be implying it does not, it means that between August-
Shame.

-of 1958 and March of 1959 the department had done certain work and he had then asked them to do some more work. What we want to know is what that work was; how much it cost; how many people were engaged on it and how many people have been engaged on it since.
The minister just said there was none.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Because the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate makes assertions like this I am very tempted to reply in kind; but I hope this is my good day in the House of Commons and I assure him that no matter the provocation he cannot get me ruffled one bit.
Why don't you give it to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Someone says "Give it to him". I do not think so at all. We are getting on nicely and I am getting complete co-operation from the opposition. But what the Minister of Transport said on August 4 or on any other day I know nothing about.
You are a member of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I know what I read in Hansard of March 4, 1959 does not by any stretch of the imagination indicate anything else but what I have already told the committee, and I repeat it again, that the Department of
6624	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works Public Works have not done any economic survey since our government took office.
I hope the hon. member does not think I am trying to mislead him when I talk about an economic survey or a feasibility survey. I certainly will not be caught again by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate like on that embarrassing day in this house when the press had the statement about General Young's forthcoming visit. That is the situation and there is nothing I can add. I cannot interpret the mind of the Minister of Transport; he is always amply able to defend himself.

The minister said earlier, and if I misinterpret what he said he will correct me at once, that when he referred to the arrangement with Mr. Flemming the government yielded to the importunings of the premier of New Brunswick notwithstanding the fact that many feasibility studies had been previously made. Could the minister tell us what feasibility studies he was talking about when he said that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: As the Minister of Transport said, this matter was very prominently discussed way back in 1822. There has certainly been none undertaken since the Liberal government got into power in 1935. As a matter of fact, I am informed, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will correct me if I am wrong, that the Hon. George Marler, the former minister of transport, at the 1959 Liberal convention opposed a resolution in favour of the Chignecto canal.

I can give the minister information about that if he wants it. It has nothing to do with the estimates of the Department of Public Works, but the position taken by Mr. Marler was a not unintelligent position. He said he thought a study should be made before the party committed itself to doing the thing.
However, the Prime Minister was very specific and I will take a report from the Saint John Telegraph-Journal which will per. haps reassure the Minister of Veterans Affairs a little more.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What book is that you are going to quote from?
This is a volume which was produced in the interests of history-
Oh, oh.

-by the national Liberal federation so that this country would have on record some of the promises made by the right hon. gentleman who bought his way into office in this country with promises, most of which he did not keep.
Oh, oh, shame.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Did the hon. member make the statement that the Prime Minister bought his way in?
Mr. Chairman, I have the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am rising on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I want to remind hon. members we are on vote 327 of the public works estimates and I would suggest that hon. members please come back to it. The Chair has been quite lenient.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, the statement made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate cannot remain unchallenged and I think it should be withdrawn immediately.

That is no question of
privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is a point of order then.

It is certainly not a point of order. It is a debating point which the hon. minister has a perfect right to debate if he wants to, but notwithstanding that fact I think I was in error in saying that the Prime Minister bought his way into office. I think too highly of the Canadian people. The Prime Minister talked his way into office because the Canadian people wrongly believed the things he said.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I hope I will not have to remind hon. members again to please come back to vote 327.

I think this study which was promised by the Prime Minister-another of those promises which he did not keep-has directly to do with this department because as the Minister of Transport told us, rightly or wrongly, he said he would ask the Department of Public Works to make this study. They apparently do not know anything about that request, but he said he would ask them and that is in Hansard and was read by the Minister of Public Works himself.
Here is another extract of this promise of the Prime Minister's on May 3, 1957, another of these assurances that the Prime Minister said he always keeps:
Investigation of the feasibility of a Chignecto canal connecting the bay of Fundy and Northumberland strait was promised Friday night by John Diefenbaker if a Progressive Conservative government is elected.
"Our intention is to give it the widest possible investigation,"

And so on. The report continues:
Mr. Diefenbaker said he considered the canal part of the St. Lawrence seaway system. The survey would determine "whether the dream of past generations can become the reality of the future."
That promise was made three years ago. Three years later on the eve of a provincial election this government's idea of keeping that promise is to screw half the cost of the study the Prime Minister promised out of the provincial treasury of that province. It is no wonder that Mr. Flemming went down to defeat if that is the way this government treats its friends.

This past half hour has been a most interesting discussion about who would pay for what in the planning of the Chignecto canal. I have no objection whatever to any work undertaken in the maritimes or any planning done in the maritimes; but after listening this last half hour I cannot help but wonder whether we ever remember that there is also a Pacific coast.
If it is of such importance, as it undoubtedly is, that a connection by the Chignecto canal be paid 100 per cent by the federal government, in view of the fact that although the maritimes has been a depressed area and I think has had pretty fine consideration from this House of Commons over these last two or three years-
Hear, hear.

-we on the Pacific coast under similar circumstances do not get the same treatment.
So I would like to ask the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, if I am in order in asking this question, because we are a nation, not a series of Balkan states. In British Columbia we have Vancouver island off the Pacific coast. It is 72 miles wide and I think about 370 miles long, with I believe just under 200,000 of population. Would the minister also give us the same treatment in British Columbia as he gives the maritimes on their Chignecto canal and make an engineering survey or a feasibility survey of a causeway from the lower mainland of British Columbia to Vancouver island? We do not ask for privileges. We ask for equality.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
So that the record may be complete and final, and to add to the evidence which has already been put on record by the Minister of Transport which has not impressed the Minister of Public Works, perhaps I might remind the hon. gentleman of some evidence given by his predecessor as minister of public works who when asked on June 13, 1958, as reported on page 1139 of 79951-0-418i
Supply-Public Works Hansard, whether the government was doing anything about the Chignecto canal, replied:
Well, it is under study.
Then when the subject came up again a few days later on June 19, 1958, the hon. member for Gloucester had this to say:
On June 13, the minister said the Chignecto canal is being studied by his department. Is the minister in a position to report to this committee what action has been taken thus far in connection with the canal?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. The study is still under way.
How far has the study been carried? Have any engineers of the department been instructed to make preliminary plans?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This study is being carried on within the department, and I am afraid I cannot go any further than that.
This is the study which the present minister said is not being undertaken and has not been undertaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No engineers, as the hon. gentleman knows, have been appointed, and what they are studying are the possibilities of having a feasibility survey, I would take it. If I have been wrong, then I am sorry, but the fact remains that there has been no feasibility survey in the Department of Public Works.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Now the minister is saying that the study is on the question of whether there will be a study. That is the study which has been going on for three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am going to study, as a result of the observations of many hon. members on both sides of the house; whether or not I am going to undertake certain feasibility projects, I am going to do a lot of studying. That would not mean I am going to do a lot of undertaking, the fact that I am studying-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister was always a good student.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Thank you, professor.

Since the government is undertaking studies in connection with the Prince Edward Island causeway and in connection with the Chignecto canal, will the minister give the same opportunities to British Columbia and study the feasibility of a connecting link between the lower mainland of British Columbia and Vancouver island?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I know the hon. member for Vancouver East desires an answer, though I hate to take up the time of the committee. We always consider carefully the requests of the provincial government of British Columbia which, under its present administration, has never been modest in its demands. I

Supply-Public Works can assure the committee that at no time have we ever been asked for such a survey, but if the hon. member would like to get in touch with his friends the Social Credit government-
I am sorry. They are not my friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We have a peculiar habit in this house of referring to people as our friends when they are sometimes our deadly enemies. Perhaps that applies in the case of the hon. member, though not, of course, in a personal sense. That province which, according to its premier, has no funded debt, is always complaining that it is not getting enough, but as one example I would point out that of the $400 million being spent by the dominion government on the trans-Canada highway the province of British Columbia is getting more than one quarter of the total.
I would point out to the minister that we have a range of mountains there.

There seem to be a number of contradictory reports with regard to this Chignecto canal survey, and I wish to place on the record the following exchange which is reported on page 243 of Hansard of January 23, 1959. It reads as follows:

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Is the minister now prepared to report to the house on the progress of the cost survey of the Chignecto canal to be undertaken by the Department of Public Works, as announced in this house on August 28 last, when he promised to report at a later date?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The answer, Mr. Speaker, is no.
I have a supplementary question. Has the survey been undertaken?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The survey certainly has not been completed. I will confer with my colleague the Minister of Public Works to find out what is the position.
Has it been started?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I told the hon. member X would speak to my colleague. Perhaps the Minister of Public Works will answer now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member will check his Hansard for last year I think he will find that I said a study had been undertaken by the department.
Is the Minister of Public Works prepared to report on the progress of that survey?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No.
Again I wish to repeat that this house has been led to believe for the last two and a half or three years that a survey was under way by the department.

I have been asking the minister time after time the name of the one who made the investigation in the case in which, as hon. members know, I am interested. I

do so because an injustice has been committed against a person who did not deserve it and I have the proof here that the investigation which was undertaken was a very poor one, if it is the same man to whom the investigation referred. Here I have proof that the investigation was very badly made by the investigator of the department, if there was one. I have a letter from the Banque Cana-dienne Nationale stating that they were satisfied with the work that had been done there.
The minister spoke this afternoon of the work at Mont Joli, which was work covering a vault over stairs and garage a couple of years ago and said that it was very badly executed, that the roof leaked, that there was extremely bad plumbing, that windows were fixed with nails instead of screws and so on. Yet here I have a letter stating the contrary, and if the minister has taken any action against this man on the basis of a report coming from such a quarter I am sorry, because the man who sent in that report had no conscience at all. He did not go to the real persons in order to ask about this affair. He did not go to the chief architect of the Banque Canadienne Nationale in which case he would have got a completely different statement. This is an injustice, and the minister should repair that injustice in favour of that man.

Well done.
Another hon. Member: Politics.

Who said "politics"? If there is one politician who is acting only for political purposes it is the present minister because he made that to please one member and all these things which have been said are just said to please the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulange who wanted his man to have the contract.

Well done.
(Translation):
Another hon. Member: The minister said it was out of order.
Who talks about being out of order? If the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) wants to discuss points of order in French, I shall be pleased to do so.
You are not a lawyer.
I do not have to be a lawyer; I can understand justice better than the Minister of Public Works.
What does the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) think of renting space in his building to the telegraph division of the C.N.R.? I think that is disgraceful for a member of parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Chairman, I am being directly taken to task by the member lor Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). Let me tell him this: whenever the hon. member wants to discuss that point, let him say so, and I will prove to him that I am more familiar than he is with the Senate and House of Commons act.
(Text):

I have some questions; I have not a speech to make, but I have some questions about the general administration of the department which can only be asked on the administrative item, that I would now like to put to the minister but I do not want to interfere with any other hon. member who has any speech to make. I am putting questions that I should like answers to because on the answers will depend further questions that I wish to ask.
The first question that I should like to put to the Minister of Public Works is who is the chief architect of the Department of Public Works and when was he appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I will answer them all at one time.
I am afraid that is not very convenient because I want the answers in order to pose certain other questions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is a simple one: you ought to be able to answer it.
I think the minister is going to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Quite so; I will be delighted. The chief architect is Mr. E. A. Gardner, and I think the year of his appointment was 1952.
He was appointed chief architect in 1952?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I know my hon. friend will appreciate my saying this, that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George was not too young to win the military cross and bar away back in 1943.

The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is not too young to make from time to time very distinguished and very good natured contributions to the debates of the House of Commons. The question I was asking some little time ago and which I will now resume for the benefit of the minister was as to all those projects since June 21, 1957 where more than one contract was called for a particular project and the reason for departing from the principle enunciated by the minister, namely that a plan for a project must be completed before the contract was called and that a single contract called for the whole project if there was not to be a horrible mess-to quote his words-in the administration of the department. I do not want to involve him in things that were not started by the present government. Perhaps I should amend this date to April 1, 1958. Then I wish the minister to tell us about the Jackson building. We know there was an explosion near the Jackson building. I am not blaming the minister or the government for that explosion. However, we know there was an explosion, that the employees had to be moved out and that the building had to be renovated. I should like the minister to go through the various steps in connection with this matter. I should like him to tell us whether a complete plan was prepared for the renovation of this building before any work was done, whether tenders were called, whether there was a single tender for the whole job and whether there were any extras.
I should also like the minister to tell us this. Here, Mr. Chairman, I am talking about something that happened since the public accounts committee had experience with the printing bureau. eventually awarded; what the contract was; whether the contract was satisfactorily performed and whether it is functioning properly at the present time.

I expect the answers during the course of consideration of the estimates, of course. These questions are of a kind that the hon. gentleman and his friends used to ask of ministers. I can remember some of the questions that were asked of Mr. Fournier when he was sitting over there on the other side of the chamber and also of Mr. Winters when the previous government was in office. My hon. friends felt it was their duty to have the information about the affairs of all departments at their fingertips-the questions were far more voluminous with all these details in them-and it did not take hours and hours and hours.
After all, I have confined these questions to matters which are exceptional. I should draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that I have confined these questions precisely and exclusively to those matters-except for my first question-which are exceptional. I have not asked about any case where one contract was let for the whole project and whether it was performed within the scope of the whole contract. Under the wellnigh perfect administration of this department which we are led to believe there has been since 1957 I cannot believe that the number of exceptions would be much more than can be counted on the fingers of two hands. I think the committee as well as the country will be surprised if the minister preached one thing and practised another.
That is precisely why I am asking this question. I am asking this question in order to see how close the minister has kept to that principle he enunciated a couple of years ago, namely that it was bad business, bad administration and bad for the treasury to call a tender until the plans were completed, until an estimate from the department was available, and then one single tender should be called for the whole project and that any other procedure was unbusinesslike and improper. Those were the principles the minister enunciated very clearly as the guiding principles for the biggest construction department of the government or one of the biggest construction departments.

It is true, of course, that the Minister of Transport follows an entirely different principle, as he has told us over and over again. He is not a bit impressed by these views of the Minister of Public Works. He blithely lets dozens of contracts for the same project and they seem to grow and multiply and the cost grows and multiplies with them. But I suppose it is like this other case we had earlier of the right hand not knowing what the left hand was doing.
However, in view of the high principles enunciated by the minister, Mr. Chairman, I say that the committee is entitled to know whether they are being carried out.

I was most amused to observe the great effort that the pot made to label the kettle black. When it comes to the matter of awarding contracts in the Department of Public Works I think the Liberal record is so lousy that it smells to high heaven. The Canadian electorate at the last election knew what they ought to do with that Liberal record. I think it ill behooves the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to attempt now to interrogate the relatively new Minister of Public Works on awards that have been offered because, as he well knows, the minister has not been in office for very long.
This is a rather rare occasion in my life's history, Mr. Chairman, because whatever there is in me that is good or bad I have to ascribe it not only to myself but to my parents and to my mentors. I have in the gallery here this evening two of my former school teachers, namely Messrs. Epp and Bergen and I want to pay my respects to them.
To return to the issue, I notice with considerable dismay that the Minister of Public Works has been obliged to suffer a reduction in the amount of money allotted to him, I assume because of the orders of his colleague the Minister of Finance. The reduction is from $226 million to $195 million. As many other members who have preceded me have stated, at a time when there is mass unemployment in the nation I feel that this reduction is most unwise and ought not to have been undertaken at this time. If anything, in order to relieve the employment situation I feel there ought to have been an expansion in the amount of money made available to the minister at this time.
I notice in particular that he has been reduced in the amount of money that is available to him with regard to public buildings construction and services. Whereas a year ago the department was allowed to spend $50 million, this year it is being permitted to spend only $34 million. I also notice that under harbours and rivers, engineering services, whereas a year ago the department was
Supply-Public Works permitted to spend $33 million this year it is permitted to spend only $26 million. I can understand that there may be circumstances when a reduction in public spending may be advisable. However, at a time of mass unemployment I feel it is most unwise to reduce expenditures in the field of erecting new public buildings and in the field of harbours and rivers engineering services.
I hope the minister will be able to tell us why the amounts of the votes this year are identical with the votes of a year ago. I have particular reference to vote 355, which is to the extent of $2,800,000 exactly what it was a year ago, and also to vote 356 which is $3,606,075, again identical with the amount allocated a year ago. I have looked over the details and I notice there is a variation. Knowing the minister to be an honest and well meaning man I would like to ask him how, with increased wages which are acknowledged in the details and increases here and there, he yet manages to arrive at the identical number of dollars.
It reminds me of an occasion a number of years ago when the former member for Nanaimo completely floored the Liberal minister of national defence of that day when he called attention to the fact that the estimates of national defence were identical even to the last dollar to what they were the year before.
In other words, this indicates a certain sloppiness in the department. It indicates that a departmental official has authorized the spending of as much as was spent last year but no more. I know that the minister has been under the axe of the Minister of Finance and his over-all expenditure is much less. The minister is only being allowed, even in the light of the unemployment situation today, to spend $195 million whereas a year ago he was permitted to spend $226 million.
However, as I said, the over-all amount is identical and unless the minister has a real explanation to offer it indicates sloppiness on the part of someone in his department. I have particular reference to vote 355, which is identical with the same vote of a year ago even though the details are not identical, and vote 356 which is identical with what it was a year ago although the details reveal there are alterations. But I think the minister is called to account to this committee how in the world he manages to end up with exactly the same amount of money.

I only have one question to ask the minister and it has to do with personnel. Can the minister tell us what is the regular staff in the architect district office in Montreal? Also, has there been any increase in the number of supervisors and foremen?

speechtext: I do not mind doing that but I would not want to be held up on the estimates for that reason. I am informed that it would take at least a week. There is a tremendous amount of research to be accurate for the hon. member. That is on the first of his major questions. I will be very happy to get the information if the hon. member will wait for it, because it is more like an order for return, is it not?

As far as the first question is concerned I suggest a very simple way of doing it would be to take the blue books for the last three years and look at every project listed of over $100,000. It does not seem to me to be a very big task but I may not understand these things. In any event, if the minister gives an undertaking to provide the information as soon as it can conveniently be made available I would be satisfied with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I would be glad to get the information for the hon. member for Levis as well; I do not think it will take very long.
I would not like to hold up the passage of this item and I agree, if the information will be ready tomorrow. But I may have some remarks to make on that and I hope I will be allowed to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
In reply to the matters raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam with regard to items 355 and 356, surely he appreciates we have to have something in reserve. We never know when there will be a storm or some act of God, or some sudden happening or emergency which we have not been able to anticipate. That is why we usually put in a little more than we expect

to spend. We try to get a figure which we have found from our experience in the past to be an adequate one and I think it is safe to say that we are not doing a good job on the estimates if we actually spend in a year as much as we put into these particular items because we have to have a reserve for emergency. Does that answer the question?

I want to thank the minister for his answer and to ask him a further question about another matter. The hon. gentleman's predecessor announced it was no longer the policy of the government for the Department of Public Works to take a lease enabling a person to erect a public building for the purpose of renting it to the government over a fixed period of years. I should like to know whether this policy still obtains or whether it has been altered since the advent of the new minister.
I know a number of instances where individuals have entered into an agreement with the Department of Public Works whereby the government undertook to pay so many dollars a month for the facilities which they needed over a stated number of years, and the man concerned was then able to go to a bank with the signed lease and get the whole of the money necessary in order to put up the building, which up to then had not even existed, and at the end of seven, eight or nine years the rentals which had been assigned to the bank against the loan had accounted for all the principal together with the interest, and the originator of the scheme was left holding the real estate and continued either to milk the public first by collecting further rentals, or to dispose of his property in another manner. I have a couple of particular enterprises in mind, and I should like to ask the minister whether the clear announcement of government policy by his predecessor, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, is equally valid today.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is perfectly right. The policy of the government is to build its own buildings. That is still the policy; to make the capital expenditure and do the best we can. Otherwise, we are mortgaging our future as has been done in some states of the union and also in one of our provinces. If you ask an entrepreneur to put up a building for you and then pay him over a period of years we find that it is usually an expensive procedure in the long run. However, there are occasions when it is advantageous to enter into a five-year lease. We do not even do that more than we can help, but if there is an interim period while things are being adjusted we find it sometimes pays us to do that rather than put up a building for the interim period.

I wish to express my appreciation to the minister for his reiteration of the policy announced by his predecessor. As he well knows, this is one of the main sources of campaign funds of the Liberal party in British Columbia, at least in years gone by and I hope he will look into the economics of the rental agreement which the department now has with the owner of the Port Moody post office and that at an early date he will negotiate the purchase of that building, because on a square foot basis he is now paying one of the highest rentals that is being paid anywhere in the dominion of Canada. I know the owner is most anxious to dispose of the property. The lease expires next year and I hope the government will begin at once to negotiate with the owner in order to avoid a continuation of an unduly high rental expenditure on the part of the taxpayers of Canada.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
